How much powder must be dissolved in $8.6$ liters of water to make fertilizer?

$\,$grams of powder must be dissolved in $8.6$ liters of water.
question.worked_solution:
To determine the amount of powder that must be dissolved in $8.6$ liters of water, we have to multiply $8.6$ by $5.5.$

We proceed by multiplying the two numbers just as we would with whole numbers.

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{aligned} &  &  &  & \,\,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{3} \\ \boxed{3}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\begin{aligned}\boxed{} \\ \boxed{0}\end{aligned}\,\,\,\, &  \\  &  &  &  & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.6\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,\times \,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,5\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,.5\,\,\,\, \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\  & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,4\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,7\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\,\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

We now count the total number of decimal places in the two factors.

There is $1$ decimal place in $8.6$ and there is $1$ decimal place in $5.5.$
Therefore, their product will have $1+1=2$ decimal places.

So, we take our value of $4730$ and add a decimal point to make a number with $2$ decimal places.

$$
47\,\overset{↓}{.}\,\,\,{{30}_{⏟}}_{2\text{ digits}}
$$

Hence, $8.6\times 5.5=47.30=47.3.$

We conclude that $47.3$ grams of powder must be dissolved in $8.6$ liters of water.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Orlando had $(10\,\frac{1}{2}-9\,\frac{1}{6})$ liters of liquid fertilizer left over.

Writing $10\,\frac{1}{2}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
10\,\frac{1}{2}=\frac{10\times 2+1}{2}=\frac{21}{2}.
$$

Writing $9\,\frac{1}{6}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
9\,\frac{1}{6}=\frac{9\times 6+1}{6}=\frac{55}{6}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{21}{2}-\frac{55}{6}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $6.$

To put $\frac{21}{2}$ over a denominator of $6,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $3:$

$$
\frac{21}{2}=\frac{21\times 3}{2\times 3}=\frac{63}{6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{63}{6}-\frac{55}{6}=\frac{8}{6}
$$

Simplifying, we have

$$
\frac{8}{6}=\frac{8÷2}{6÷2}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{4}{3}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore, Orlando had $1\,\frac{1}{3}$ liters of liquid fertilizer left over.

To determine the amount of powder Orlando used, we need to calculate the sum $0.3+0.18.$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned} &  & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,3\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, \\ \,\,\,\,+\,\,\,\, &  & \,\,\,\,0\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,1\,\,\,\, & \,\,\,\,8\,\,\,\, \\  &  &  & \,\,\,\,.\,\,\,\, &  & \end{aligned}

$$

Therefore, Orlando used $0.48\,\text{kg}$ of powdered fertilizer.

question.problem:
During a particular weekend, Orlando made $10\,\frac{1}{2}$ liters of liquid fertilizer. He used $9\,\frac{1}{6}$ liters from this amount. How much liquid fertilizer did Orlando have left over? Express your answer as a mixed number in its lowest terms.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        Orlando had$\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        
$\,$liters of liquid fertilizer left over.
question.worked_solution:
Orlando had $(10\,\frac{1}{2}-9\,\frac{1}{6})$ liters of liquid fertilizer left over.

Writing $10\,\frac{1}{2}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
10\,\frac{1}{2}=\frac{10\times 2+1}{2}=\frac{21}{2}.
$$

Writing $9\,\frac{1}{6}$ as an improper fraction, we have

$$
9\,\frac{1}{6}=\frac{9\times 6+1}{6}=\frac{55}{6}.
$$

Therefore, our problem now is to work out the following:

$$
\frac{21}{2}-\frac{55}{6}
$$

To subtract two fractions with unlike denominators, we need to express each fraction as an equivalent fraction with a common denominator.

In this question, we can make a common denominator of $6.$

To put $\frac{21}{2}$ over a denominator of $6,$ we multiply the numerator and denominator by $3:$

$$
\frac{21}{2}=\frac{21\times 3}{2\times 3}=\frac{63}{6}
$$

We can now subtract the fractions. We keep the denominator the same, and we subtract the numerators:

$$
\frac{63}{6}-\frac{55}{6}=\frac{8}{6}
$$

Simplifying, we have

$$
\frac{8}{6}=\frac{8÷2}{6÷2}=\frac{4}{3}.
$$

Finally, we convert back to a mixed number:

$$
\frac{4}{3}=1\,\text{R}\,1=1\,\frac{1}{3}
$$

Therefore, Orlando had $1\,\frac{1}{3}$ liters of liquid fertilizer left over.

question.problem:
Orlando bought $6$ packages of powdered fertilizer, for which he paid $$96.44.$ Estimate the price of each package by rounding the amount of money he spent to the nearest dollar.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        The approximate price of each package is $

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        .
question.worked_solution:
To estimate the price of each package, we need to find an approximation to $96.44÷6.$

So, we round the dividend to the nearest whole number:

$$
96.44\to 96
$$

Now, we divide $96$ by $6$ as usual:

$$
96÷6=16
$$

Therefore, the approximate price of each package is $$16.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed between the curves $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ above the line $y=2.$ What is ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA\,$ expressed as a repeated integral?
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/4e58d7969f0b31206ae8c3385a857c0ad6cf8a42ee79909d51c3a6b58a090852.png)

We need to represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ y & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=2,$ the $y$-limits are 
$2\le y\le 4.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/16944d6651297f1c13c39ddf3d9160d721f5f29bfa6b0acac0db46c88295964e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed between the curves y=2x and y=x2 above the line y=2. What is ∬Df(x,y)dA expressed as a repeated integral?

questions.knowledge_point: Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given
questions.raw_html:
1.Representing a Double Integral as a Repeated Integral When the Limits are Not Given?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed between the curves y=2x and y=x2 above the line y=2. What is ∬Df(x,y)dA expressed as a repeated integral?

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/c3dbd6e26cb67b2f247387c30e03296f790c3f56c03779a7dda5ae5d0b081958.png)

If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines $x=3-{y}^{3},\,$ $x={y}^{3},$ and $y=0,$ as shown above, then ${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/366146b42d476b8d2a467e607a3bba1ef65ddc8a344b3f0e17ee4652ccc0463a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}},\,{y}^{3}\le x\le 3-{y}^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}(y-1)\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}\,dx]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)\,[x]_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)({y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-{y}^{4}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-{y}^{4}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={[-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Calculate ${\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dx\,dy.$
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}{\int }_{0}^{y}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{y}dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}[x]_{0}^{y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}(y-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}y\,\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}}y\operatorname{cos}⁡{y}^{2}\,dy & ={[\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡{y}^{2}}{2}]}_{0}^{\sqrt{3\pi /2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type II region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,2{y}^{2}\le x\le {y}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[\,x\,]_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y({y}^{2}+1-2{y}^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type II Region
questions.raw_html:
5.Calculating a Double Integral Defined Over a Type II Region?

Calculate ∬DydA, where D={(x,y):0≤y≤1,2y2≤x≤y2+1}.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/4e58d7969f0b31206ae8c3385a857c0ad6cf8a42ee79909d51c3a6b58a090852.png)

We need to represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ y & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=2,$ the $y$-limits are 
$2\le y\le 4.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/16944d6651297f1c13c39ddf3d9160d721f5f29bfa6b0acac0db46c88295964e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed between the curves y=2x and y=x2 above the line y=2. What is ∬Df(x,y)dA expressed as a repeated integral?

a
∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy
b
∫2y/2∫0yf(x,y)dxdy
c
∫0y∫2y/2f(x,y)dxdy
d
∫24∫yy/2f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫2y∫0y/2f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

We need to represent D as a type II region. Writing y=2x and y=x2 in terms of y, we obtain

y=2x⟹x=y2y=x2⟹x=y

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: y=y2y=y24y2−4y=0y(y−4)=0 So, since our region lies above the line y=2, the y-limits are 2≤y≤4.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):2≤y≤4,y2≤x≤y}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬Df(x,y)dA=∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/366146b42d476b8d2a467e607a3bba1ef65ddc8a344b3f0e17ee4652ccc0463a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}},\,{y}^{3}\le x\le 3-{y}^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

If D is the finite region enclosed by the lines x=3−y3, x=y3, and y=0, as shown above, then ∬D1xydA=

a
∫03/23[∫y33−y31xydx]dy
b
∫03/23[∫3−y3y31xydx]dy
c
∫03−y3[∫y33/231xydx]dy
d
∫y33−y3[∫03/231xydx]dy
e
∫y33/23[∫03−y31xydx]dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's represent D as a type II region.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: 3−y3=y32y3=3y3=32y=323 So, y-limits are 0≤y≤323.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):0≤y≤323,y3≤x≤3−y3}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬D1xydA=∫03/23∫y33−y31xydxdy=∫03/23[∫y33−y31xydx]dy

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type II region.

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}(y-1)\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}\,dx]\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)\,[x]_{{y}^{3}}^{{y}^{2}}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-1)({y}^{2}-{y}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(-{y}^{4}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-{y}^{4}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={[-\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}+\frac{{y}^{4}}{2}-\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{3} \\  & =-\frac{1}{30}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[\,x\,]_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y({y}^{2}+1-2{y}^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy\end{aligned}

$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed between the curves $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ above the line $y=2.$ What is ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA\,$ expressed as a repeated integral?
question.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/4e58d7969f0b31206ae8c3385a857c0ad6cf8a42ee79909d51c3a6b58a090852.png)

We need to represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ y & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=2,$ the $y$-limits are 
$2\le y\le 4.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/16944d6651297f1c13c39ddf3d9160d721f5f29bfa6b0acac0db46c88295964e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed between the curves y=2x and y=x2 above the line y=2. What is ∬Df(x,y)dA expressed as a repeated integral?

a
∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy
b
∫2y/2∫0yf(x,y)dxdy
c
∫0y∫2y/2f(x,y)dxdy
d
∫24∫yy/2f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫2y∫0y/2f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

We need to represent D as a type II region. Writing y=2x and y=x2 in terms of y, we obtain

y=2x⟹x=y2y=x2⟹x=y

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: y=y2y=y24y2−4y=0y(y−4)=0 So, since our region lies above the line y=2, the y-limits are 2≤y≤4.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):2≤y≤4,y2≤x≤y}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬Df(x,y)dA=∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/4e58d7969f0b31206ae8c3385a857c0ad6cf8a42ee79909d51c3a6b58a090852.png)

We need to represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ y & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=2,$ the $y$-limits are 
$2\le y\le 4.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/16944d6651297f1c13c39ddf3d9160d721f5f29bfa6b0acac0db46c88295964e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed between the curves y=2x and y=x2 above the line y=2. What is ∬Df(x,y)dA expressed as a repeated integral?

a
∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy
b
∫2y/2∫0yf(x,y)dxdy
c
∫0y∫2y/2f(x,y)dxdy
d
∫24∫yy/2f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫2y∫0y/2f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

We need to represent D as a type II region. Writing y=2x and y=x2 in terms of y, we obtain

y=2x⟹x=y2y=x2⟹x=y

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: y=y2y=y24y2−4y=0y(y−4)=0 So, since our region lies above the line y=2, the y-limits are 2≤y≤4.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):2≤y≤4,y2≤x≤y}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬Df(x,y)dA=∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy

solution.reasoning: The curves intersect at (0,0) and (2,4). Above y=2, the region has 2≤y≤4. Each horizontal slice runs from x=y/2 to x=\sqrt{y}, so option a is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem: Consider the finite region $D$ in the $xy$-plane enclosed between the curves $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ above the line $y=2.$ What is ${∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA\,$ expressed as a repeated integral?
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's make a sketch of our region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/4e58d7969f0b31206ae8c3385a857c0ad6cf8a42ee79909d51c3a6b58a090852.png)

We need to represent $D$ as a type II region. Writing $y=2x$ and $y={x}^{2}$ in terms of $y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}y=2x & \,⟹\,x=\frac{y}{2} \\ y={x}^{2} & \,⟹\,x=\sqrt{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{y} & =\frac{y}{2} \\ y & =\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} \\ {y}^{2}-4y & =0 \\ y(y-4) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

So, since our region lies above the line $y=2,$ the $y$-limits are 
$2\le y\le 4.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/16944d6651297f1c13c39ddf3d9160d721f5f29bfa6b0acac0db46c88295964e.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,2\le y\le 4,\,\frac{y}{2}\le x\le \sqrt{y}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dA & ={\int }_{2}^{4}{\int }_{y/2}^{\sqrt{y}}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Consider the finite region D in the xy-plane enclosed between the curves y=2x and y=x2 above the line y=2. What is ∬Df(x,y)dA expressed as a repeated integral?

a
∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy
b
∫2y/2∫0yf(x,y)dxdy
c
∫0y∫2y/2f(x,y)dxdy
d
∫24∫yy/2f(x,y)dxdy
e
∫2y∫0y/2f(x,y)dxdy
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's make a sketch of our region.

We need to represent D as a type II region. Writing y=2x and y=x2 in terms of y, we obtain

y=2x⟹x=y2y=x2⟹x=y

Now, let's determine the limits of integration.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: y=y2y=y24y2−4y=0y(y−4)=0 So, since our region lies above the line y=2, the y-limits are 2≤y≤4.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):2≤y≤4,y2≤x≤y}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬Df(x,y)dA=∫24∫y/2yf(x,y)dxdy

question.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/366146b42d476b8d2a467e607a3bba1ef65ddc8a344b3f0e17ee4652ccc0463a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}},\,{y}^{3}\le x\le 3-{y}^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If D is the finite region enclosed by the lines x=3−y3, x=y3, and y=0, as shown above, then ∬D1xydA=

a
∫03/23[∫y33−y31xydx]dy
b
∫03/23[∫3−y3y31xydx]dy
c
∫03−y3[∫y33/231xydx]dy
d
∫y33−y3[∫03/231xydx]dy
e
∫y33/23[∫03−y31xydx]dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's represent D as a type II region.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: 3−y3=y32y3=3y3=32y=323 So, y-limits are 0≤y≤323.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):0≤y≤323,y3≤x≤3−y3}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬D1xydA=∫03/23∫y33−y31xydxdy=∫03/23[∫y33−y31xydx]dy

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/366146b42d476b8d2a467e607a3bba1ef65ddc8a344b3f0e17ee4652ccc0463a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}},\,{y}^{3}\le x\le 3-{y}^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

If D is the finite region enclosed by the lines x=3−y3, x=y3, and y=0, as shown above, then ∬D1xydA=

a
∫03/23[∫y33−y31xydx]dy
b
∫03/23[∫3−y3y31xydx]dy
c
∫03−y3[∫y33/231xydx]dy
d
∫y33−y3[∫03/231xydx]dy
e
∫y33/23[∫03−y31xydx]dy
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's represent D as a type II region.

  • To determine the y-limits, we need to find the y-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for y: 3−y3=y32y3=3y3=32y=323 So, y-limits are 0≤y≤323.

  • To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

As a result, we get

D={(x,y):0≤y≤323,y3≤x≤3−y3}.

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

∬D1xydA=∫03/23∫y33−y31xydxdy=∫03/23[∫y33−y31xydx]dy

solution.reasoning: The curves meet where y^3=3-y^3, giving y=\sqrt[3]{3/2}. For 0≤y≤\sqrt[3]{3/2}, each horizontal slice extends from x=y^3 to x=3-y^3. Thus option a gives the correct repeated integral, interpreted as an improper integral at the boundary singularities. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

If $D$ is the finite region enclosed by the lines $x=3-{y}^{3},\,$ $x={y}^{3},$ and $y=0,$ as shown above, then ${∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's represent $D$ as a type II region. 

- To determine the $y$-limits, we need to find the $y$-coordinates of the points at which the curves intersect. So, we set the following equation and solve it for $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3-{y}^{3} & ={y}^{3} \\ 2{y}^{3} & =3 \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{3}{2} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

So, $y$-limits are 
$0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}}.$

- To determine the left and right functions, we draw a horizontal arrow from left to right through the region, as usual.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159301/assets/366146b42d476b8d2a467e607a3bba1ef65ddc8a344b3f0e17ee4652ccc0463a.png)

As a result, we get

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le \sqrt[3]{\frac{3}{2}},\,{y}^{3}\le x\le 3-{y}^{3}\}.
$$

Therefore, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\sqrt[3]{3/2}}[{\int }_{{y}^{3}}^{3-{y}^{3}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{xy}}\,dx]dy\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate ∬DydA, where D={(x,y):0≤y≤1,2y2≤x≤y2+1}.

a
 18
b
 32
c
 4
d
 14
e
 2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The integral is defined over a type II region D={(x,y):0≤y≤1,2y2≤x≤y2+1}.

So, we can express the integral as follows:

∬DydA=∫01∫2y2y2+1ydxdy

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to x, treating y as a constant:

∫01∫2y2y2+1ydxdy=∫01y[∫2y2y2+1dx]dy=∫01y[x]2y2y2+1dy=∫01y(y2+1−2y2)dy=∫01(y−y3)dy

Then, we integrate with respect to y:

∫01(y−y3)dy=[12y2−14y4]01=12−14=14

solution.reasoning: Integrating over x gives y[(y^2+1)-2y^2]=y-y^3. Integrating from y=0 to 1 gives 1/2-1/4=1/4, so option d is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.worked_solution:
The integral is defined over a type II region $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,2{y}^{2}\le x\le {y}^{2}+1\}.$

So, we can express the integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral by integrating with respect to $x$, treating $y$ as a constant:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}y\,dx\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[{\int }_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dx]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y[\,x\,]_{2{y}^{2}}^{{y}^{2}+1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}y({y}^{2}+1-2{y}^{2})dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-1\end{aligned}\,\,[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & a & b \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ c \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & 20 & -10 \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=20+(-10)+(-6)=4.
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}7{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=5 \\ 14{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\,[\begin{aligned}245 & 70 & a \\ 70 & 20 & 10 \\ c & 10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}35 \\ b \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}7 & 14 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 14 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}245 & 70 & 35 \\ 70 & 20 & 10 \\ 35 & 10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}35 \\ 10 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=35+10+35=80.
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ above. If the normal equation corresponding to the system $Ax=b$ is given below, what is the value of $a+b+c?$

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & 20 \\ 20 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}c \\ 8\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}10 & 20 \\ 20 & 40\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=10+40+4=54.
$$

A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ above. If the normal equation corresponding to the system $Ax=b$ is given below, what is the value of $a-b-c?$ 

$$
[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 & 36 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ b & 2 & a\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2 \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 8 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 8 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}18 & 1 & 36 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 36 & 2 & 72\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2 \\ 20\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

Therefore, we have

$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ -\frac{1}{5} \\ b\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ c \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{5}-{x}_{3}.
$$

From the first row, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}=1.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{1}{5}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot 0+(-1)=0.
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}b \\ c \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-10a+\frac{6b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}90 & -30 \\ -30 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-27 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 & -27 \\ -30 & 10 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 & -27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have  

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{10} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-10a+\frac{6b}{c}=-10\cdot (-\frac{3}{10})+\frac{6\cdot (\frac{1}{3})}{1}=5.
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-2a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-15 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

 Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-2a+\frac{b}{c}=-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=3.
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}c \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+3b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+3b+c=0+3\cdot (-2)+1=-5.
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3 \\ 2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $7a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ -28 & 56 & 8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{4b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$

$$

$$

$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}27 & -27 \\ -27 & 27\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}27 & -27 & -9 \\ -27 & 27 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}27 & -27 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-9a+\frac{b}{c}=-9\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})+\frac{1}{1}=4.
$$

$$

what is the value of $2a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$

$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-15 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.

Hence, the general solution is

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=1.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/7122f0c4dd74925137e301a4b0ac3672d1f1b30cadf19f3bce438bce202b5720.svg)

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a-b+c?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/d48e14c19cb4927af5d1199fe7a8f34ff4ddd96314f56d69534d438786dc2ff9.svg)

The normal equation corresponding to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ -3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & -2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ -3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}80 & -60 & -20 \\ -60 & 45 & 15 \\ -20 & 15 & 5\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}32 \\ -24 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-b+c=(-20)-(-24)+(-20) = -16.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Constructing the Normal Equation Corresponding to a Linear System

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/169c756c5420efe2234b3f20da794cc77e45f24c27cfafadfdf899ea9330c986.svg)

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $\mathbf{b}$ shown above. Find the general least-squares solution of the system $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 3 \\ 2 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -4 \\ -18 & 54 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
x_1=-\dfrac{2}{3}+3x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=1 \\ 2{x}_{1}-8{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+8{x}_{2}=-1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. Find the general least-squares solution of the system $A \mathbf x = \mathbf b.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/9e09cbd3d953c8ce24e0a4b8a2b37c90dc3fc00d20c008b64dd068737c6ff49e.svg)

The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 2 & -8 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & -2 \\ 4 & -8 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -36 \\ -36 & 144\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -36 & 3 \\ -36 & 144 & -12\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}9 & -36 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
x_1=\dfrac{1}{3}+ 4x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique.

tutorials.content:
Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/6bcdc34077d88eac5ed89d408a1d2525b617a4f427b13433757df918585d380f.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/b93bd5cb988f208eb26115bfaa08e81be989ee79cf3655612c1a0522a5566d95.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique.

tutorial.content:
Let's consider the following inconsistent system of equations:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/a6764d3496cf0b42005c109d539c6a44becdb9ba6ea8f1ae54c0fc20eedfaee8.svg)

Since the system is inconsistent, we cannot find an exact solution. However, as we've previously seen, we can attempt to find the so-called least-squares solution, which is a vector ${\hat{\mathbf{x}}}$ such that

$$
\|  A{\hat{\mathbf{x}}} - \mathbf{b} \|
$$

is as small as possible. 

As before, the least-squares solution can be found by solving the corresponding normal equation, given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, note the following: 

- Previously, we solved the normal equation by left-multiplying the normal equation by $(A^T A)^{-1}.$

- However, in this case, the second column of $A$ is a multiple of the first.

- So, the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent.

- Therefore, $A^T A$ is not invertible.

To solve the normal equation in this case, we proceed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,A\overset{^}{x} & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -20 \\ -20 & 80\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 20\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the last equation by Gaussian elimination, we obtain the general solution

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14159227/assets/414c827d52b8a7bdb4e713d8af2b390876859d7b01b7c527f3a83ea79752e31f.svg)

Notice that our solution is not unique! The second term of the least-squares solution (highlighted in blue) represents vectors from the null space of $A.$ 

In general, if a matrix $A$ has collinear columns, then the least-squares solution to $A\mathbf x = \mathbf b$ is not unique.

The normal equation corresponding to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ -3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & -3 & -1 \\ 8 & -6 & -2\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 8 \\ -3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}80 & -60 & -20 \\ -60 & 45 & 15 \\ -20 & 15 & 5\end{aligned}]x & =[\begin{aligned}32 \\ -24 \\ -8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a-b+c=(-20)-(-24)+(-20) = -16.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & 20 & -10 \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=20+(-10)+(-6)=4.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].

$$

$$

$$
a+b+c=35+10+35=80.

The least-squares solution of $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
A^T \! A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ -1 & 3 \\ 2 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 2 \\ -3 & 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -18 \\ -18 & 54\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -4 \\ -18 & 54 & 12\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}6 & -18 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$
x_1=-\dfrac{2}{3}+3x_2.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 \\ 0 & 5 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 & 5 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=\frac{1}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable.

From the second row, we have 

$$
{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-\frac{1}{5}-{x}_{3}.
$$

From the first row, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}=1.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{1}{5}-{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -\frac{1}{5} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+2b+c=1+2\cdot 0+(-1)=0.
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System Given in Matrix Form with Collinearity
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$

question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}b \\ c \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$
