observed_steps.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+3b+c=0+3\cdot (-2)+1=-5.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 11
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ -28 & 56 & 8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{7}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{7}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{7} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
7a+\frac{b}{c}=7\cdot (-\frac{2}{7})+\frac{2}{1}=0.
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3 \\ 2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $7a+\frac{b}{c}?$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$

\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-15 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=1.
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
4a+\frac{b}{c}=4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{1}=3.
$$

question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=-1\end{aligned}\,\,[\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & a & b \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ c \\ 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & 20 & -10 \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=20+(-10)+(-6)=4.
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 1 \\ -2 & 4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}5 & -10 & 5 \\ -10 & 20 & -10 \\ 5 & -10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=20+(-10)+(-6)=4.
$$

question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}7{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=5 \\ 14{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,\,[\begin{aligned}245 & 70 & a \\ 70 & 20 & 10 \\ c & 10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}35 \\ b \\ 5\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the system of linear equations and its corresponding normal equation shown above. What is the value of $a+b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}7 & 14 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}7 & 2 & 1 \\ 14 & 4 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 & 14 \\ 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}245 & 70 & 35 \\ 70 & 20 & 10 \\ 35 & 10 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}35 \\ 10 \\ 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$
a+b+c=35+10+35=80.
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ above. If the normal equation corresponding to the system $Ax=b$ is given below, what is the value of $a-b-c?$ 

$$
[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 & 36 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ b & 2 & a\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2 \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$
question.worked_solution:
The normal equation corresponding to $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{T}\,Ax & ={A}^{T}b \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 8 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ 4 & 0 & 8 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & 8 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}18 & 1 & 36 \\ 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 36 & 2 & 72\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}10 \\ 2 \\ 20\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a=72,\,b=36,\,c=20,
$$

and hence

$$
a-b-c=72-36-20=16.
$$

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ -\frac{1}{5} \\ b\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{3}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ c \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $a+2b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}b \\ c \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,+\,{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}a \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $2a-3b-6c?$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b.
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}12 \\ -6 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$

$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ -6 & 3 & 0 & -6 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:=2{R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}12 & -6 & 0 & 12 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(1/6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{2}:=(1/2){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable.  

From the third row, we have

$$
{x}_{3}=1,
$$

and from the first row we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1+\frac{{x}_{2}}{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a-3b-6c=2(\frac{1}{2})-3(1)-6(0)=-2.
$$

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-10a+\frac{6b}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}90 & -30 \\ -30 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-27 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 & -27 \\ -30 & 10 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 & -27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have  

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{10} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-10a+\frac{6b}{c}=-10\cdot (-\frac{3}{10})+\frac{6\cdot (\frac{1}{3})}{1}=5.
$$

question.html:
Question 8
?

A=[3−16−23−1−62],b=[−2014].

Consider the matrix A and vector b shown above. If the general least-squares solution of Ax=b is [a0]+x2[bc],x2∈R, what is the value of −10a+6bc?

a
310
b
6
c
5
d
13
e
7
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Notice that the columns of A are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

[363−6−1−2−12][3−16−23−1−62][x1x2]=[363−6−1−2−12][−2014][90−30−3010][x1x2]=[−279]

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[90−30−27−30109]R2:=R2+13R1∼[90−30−27000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we have

x1=−310+13x2.

Hence, the general solution is [−310+13x2x2]=[−3100]+x2[131],x2∈R.

Therefore, we have

−10a+6bc=−10⋅(−310)+6⋅(13)1=5.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-10a+\frac{6b}{c}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 6 & -2 \\ 3 & -1 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 6 & 3 & -6 \\ -1 & -2 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 0 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}90 & -30 \\ -30 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-27 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 & -27 \\ -30 & 10 & 9\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}90 & -30 & -27 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have  

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{10}+\frac{1}{3}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{10} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-10a+\frac{6b}{c}=-10\cdot (-\frac{3}{10})+\frac{6\cdot (\frac{1}{3})}{1}=5.
$$

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of $-2a+\frac{b}{c}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-15 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

 Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-2a+\frac{b}{c}=-2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=3.
$$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Consider the matrix $A$ and vector $b$ shown above. If the general least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}c \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+3b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+3b+c=0+3\cdot (-2)+1=-5.
$$

[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ a \\ b\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}c \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $a+3b+c?$
question.worked_solution:
The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 \\ -1 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 \\ -4 & 4 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -6 & -4 & 2 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ -4 & 4 & 4 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 & 4 & -4 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ -6 & 6 & 4 & -2 \\ 6 & -6 & -4 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-6){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+6{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has two pivot columns (the $1$st and $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{3}=-2,
$$

Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+(-2)=-1\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=-1+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-1+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0 \\ -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+3b+c=0+3\cdot (-2)+1=-5.
$$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3 \\ 2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $7a+\frac{b}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ -28 & 56 & 8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{7}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{7}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{7} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
7a+\frac{b}{c}=7\cdot (-\frac{2}{7})+\frac{2}{1}=0.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 11
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 3 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 3 \\ 2 & -4 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -28 \\ -28 & 56\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ -28 & 56 & 8\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -28 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{2}{7}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{7}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2}{7} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
7a+\frac{b}{c}=7\cdot (-\frac{2}{7})+\frac{2}{1}=0.
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

[a0]+x2[bc],x2∈R

a

EXPLANATION

First, we write our system in matrix form as Ax=b, where

A=[−122−43−6],x=[x1x2],b=[3−21].

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Notice that the columns of A are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

[−1232−4−6][−122−43−6][x1x2]=[−1232−4−6][3−21][14−28−2856][x1x2]=[−48]

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[14−28−4−28568]R2:=R2+2R1∼[14−28−4000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we have x1=−27+2x2. Hence, the general solution is

[−27+2x2x2]=[−270]+x2[21],x2∈R.

Therefore, we have

7a+bc=7⋅(−27)+21=0.

question.name: Question 12
question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $6a+\frac{4b}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$

last_observation.name: Question 12
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Least-Squares Solution of a Linear System With Collinearity
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 4 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & -2 \\ -1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}24 & -12 \\ -12 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ -12 & 6 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}24 & -12 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
6a+\frac{4b}{c}=6\cdot \frac{1}{6}+\frac{4\cdot \frac{1}{2}}{1}=3.
$$

\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 12
?

{2x1−x2=14x1−2x2=1−2x1+x2=1

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

[a0]+x2[bc],x2∈R

what is the value of 6a+4bc?

a
−1
b
2
c
1
d
4
e
3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we write our system in matrix form as Ax=b, where

A=[2−14−2−21],x=[x1x2],b=[111].

The least-squares solution of Ax=b satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

ATAx=ATb

Notice that the columns of A are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

[24−2−1−21][2−14−2−21][x1x2]=[24−2−1−21][111][24−12−126][x1x2]=[4−2]

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[24−124−126−2]R2:=R2+12R1∼[24−124000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we have x1=16+12x2. Hence, the general solution is

[16+12x2x2]=[160]+x2[121],x2∈R.

Therefore, we have

6a+4bc=6⋅16+4⋅121=3.

solution.reasoning: The normal equations reduce to 24x_1-12x_2=4, so x_1=1/6+x_2/2. Thus a=1/6, b=1/2, and c=1, giving 6a+4b/c=1+2=3, option e. The captured worked solution concerns a different example; Math Academy's answer for this question is not captured.

question.name: Question 13
question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-4 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=2 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=-3\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations shown above. If the general least-squares solution of the system is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R
$$

what is the value of $-9a+\frac{b}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}27 & -27 \\ -27 & 27\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}27 & -27 & -9 \\ -27 & 27 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}27 & -27 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-9a+\frac{b}{c}=-9\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})+\frac{1}{1}=4.
$$

First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 5 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & -1 & -5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-4 \\ 2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}27 & -27 \\ -27 & 27\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-9 \\ 9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the final matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}27 & -27 & -9 \\ -27 & 27 & 9\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}27 & -27 & -9 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{3}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
-9a+\frac{b}{c}=-9\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})+\frac{1}{1}=4.
$$

\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=-3 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=1 \\ -5{x}_{1}+10{x}_{2}=2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

what is the value of $2a+\frac{b}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2 \\ -5 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & -5 \\ -4 & -2 & 10\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}30 & -60 \\ -60 & 120\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-15 \\ 30\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ -2 & 4 & 1\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
2a+\frac{b}{c}=2\cdot (-\frac{1}{2})+\frac{2}{1}=1.
$$

$$

\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=1 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}=4 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=3\end{aligned}

First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where 

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
4a+\frac{b}{c}=4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{1}=3.
$$

First, we write our system in matrix form as $Ax=b,$ where

$$

The least-squares solution of $Ax=b$ satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

$$
{A}^{T}\,Ax={A}^{T}b
$$

Notice that the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. So first, let's write down the normal equation in matrix form:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 3 & -3 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 & -2 \\ -1 & -3 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}14 & -14 \\ -14 & 14\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ -14 & 14 & -7\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}14 & -14 & 7 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
4a+\frac{b}{c}=4\cdot (\frac{1}{2})+\frac{1}{1}=3.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: The inequality $-\sqrt{2}<x<\sqrt{2}$ can be expressed in interval notation as
questions.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints $-\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2}$ are *not* included. 

$$
-\sqrt{2}\,\,<\,\,x\,\,<\,\,\sqrt{2}
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
(-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: The inequality $-3<x<-1$ can be expressed in interval notation as
questions.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints $-3$ and $-1$ are *not* included. 

$$
-3\,\,<\,\,x\,\,<\,\,-1
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
(-3,-1)
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (-3,-1).
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which inequality corresponds to the interval $x\in [-7,0]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $(,)$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

Our interval contains only brackets. So, the endpoints *are* included. 

$$
x\in [-7,0]
$$

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

$$
-7\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,\le \,\,0
$$

x\in [-10,3].

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: The interval $y\in [-1,2)$ corresponds to the inequality
questions.worked_solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

For the given interval 

$$
[-1,2\,)
$$

we note the following:

- The left endpoint $-1$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $\le \,.$

- The right endpoint $2$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $<\,.$

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
-1\,\,\le \,\,y\,\,<\,\,2.
$$

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

$$
-5\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,<\,\,-2
$$

we note the following:

- The left endpoint $-5$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $[\,.$

- The right endpoint $-2$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $)\,.$

Therefore, the corresponding interval is

$$
x\in [-5,-2).
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses ${\color{red}{(}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{red}{)}}$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets ${\color{blue}{[}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{blue}{]}}$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

Our interval contains only parentheses. So, the endpoints are *not* included. 

$$
x\in {\color{red}{(}}1, 5{\color{red}{)}}
$$

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

$$
1 \,\,{\color{red}{<      }}\,\,      x  \,\,{\color{red}{<      }}\,\,      5
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Express the inequality $1 \le x \le4$ in interval notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses ${\color{red}{(}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{red}{)}}$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets ${\color{blue}{[}}\phantom{0} \phantom{0}{\color{blue}{]}}$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints $1$ and $4$ *are* included. 

$$
1\,\, {\color{blue}{\le}} \,\, x \,\, {\color{blue}{\le}} \,\, 4
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
{\color{blue}{[}}1,4{\color{blue}{]}}
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in [1,4].
$$

- The right endpoint $\sqrt2$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{blue}{\leq      }}\,.$

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
-4 \,\,{\color{red}{\lt  }}\,\,   y \,\,{\color{blue}{\leq}}\,\, \sqrt 2.
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the region below, which represents the inequality $2 < x < 5.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14159351/assets/feeae0bfa9b29e6f034a3fd33d1e9fbd369840835af2d6588892ee6edc2fa120.png)

We can represent this inequality using **interval notation** as follows:

$$
(2,5)
$$

The parentheses $(\phantom{0})$ tell us that the endpoints $x=2$ and $x=5$ are *not* included in this interval.

When an interval does not include the endpoints, we say that it is **open**. 

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (2,5).
$$

The symbol $\in$ means "lies in" or "belongs to." So, the above reads, "*$x$ belongs to the (open) interval $(2,5).$*"

tutorials.name: Half-Open Intervals
tutorials.problem:
Some intervals may include one parenthesis and one bracket. 

For example, consider the following interval:

$$
{\color{blue}{{\big[}}} 1,4 {\color{red}{\big)}}
$$

To express this interval as an inequality, we note the following:

- The left bracket $\,\color{blue}[\,$ tells us that left endpoint $1$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{blue}{\leq}}$ for this endpoint.

- The right parenthesis $\,\color{red})\,$ tells us that the right endpoint $4$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{red}{<      }}\,$ for this endpoint.

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
1 \,\,{\color{blue}{\leq  }}\,\,   x \,\,{\color{red}{\lt}}\,\, 4.
$$

The interval can be graphed as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14159351/assets/5a67872e8193c2bcc249a9a9006acb916909099e4babdbe5cdfa6d2643c10ad2.png)

Intervals with one bracket and one parenthesis are called **half-open** (or **half-closed**).

tutorials.content:
Some intervals may include one parenthesis and one bracket. 

For example, consider the following interval:

$$
{\color{blue}{{\big[}}} 1,4 {\color{red}{\big)}}
$$

To express this interval as an inequality, we note the following:

- The left bracket $\,\color{blue}[\,$ tells us that left endpoint $1$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{blue}{\leq}}$ for this endpoint.

- The right parenthesis $\,\color{red})\,$ tells us that the right endpoint $4$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{red}{<      }}\,$ for this endpoint.

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
1 \,\,{\color{blue}{\leq  }}\,\,   x \,\,{\color{red}{\lt}}\,\, 4.
$$

The interval can be graphed as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14159351/assets/5a67872e8193c2bcc249a9a9006acb916909099e4babdbe5cdfa6d2643c10ad2.png)

Intervals with one bracket and one parenthesis are called **half-open** (or **half-closed**).

Consider the region below, which represents the inequality $2 < x < 5.$

We can represent this inequality using **interval notation** as follows:

$$
(2,5)
$$

The parentheses $(\phantom{0})$ tell us that the endpoints $x=2$ and $x=5$ are *not* included in this interval.

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (2,5).
$$

tutorial.problem:
Some intervals may include one parenthesis and one bracket. 

For example, consider the following interval:

$$
{\color{blue}{{\big[}}} 1,4 {\color{red}{\big)}}
$$

To express this interval as an inequality, we note the following:

- The left bracket $\,\color{blue}[\,$ tells us that left endpoint $1$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{blue}{\leq}}$ for this endpoint.

- The right parenthesis $\,\color{red})\,$ tells us that the right endpoint $4$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use ${\color{red}{<      }}\,$ for this endpoint.

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
1 \,\,{\color{blue}{\leq  }}\,\,   x \,\,{\color{red}{\lt}}\,\, 4.
$$

The interval can be graphed as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14159351/assets/5a67872e8193c2bcc249a9a9006acb916909099e4babdbe5cdfa6d2643c10ad2.png)

Intervals with one bracket and one parenthesis are called **half-open** (or **half-closed**).

  • Parentheses (00) to indicate that the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] to indicate that the endpoints are included.

For the given interval

[−1,2)

we note the following:

  • The left endpoint −1 is included in the interval. Therefore, we use ≤.

  • The right endpoint 2 is not included in the interval. Therefore, we use <.

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is −1≤y<2.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: The inequality $-\sqrt{2}<x<\sqrt{2}$ can be expressed in interval notation as
question.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints $-\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2}$ are *not* included. 

$$
-\sqrt{2}\,\,<\,\,x\,\,<\,\,\sqrt{2}
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
(-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

The inequality −2<x<2 can be expressed in interval notation as

a
(−2,2)
b
[−2,2]
c
(−2,2]
d
[−2,2)
e
(−∞,2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints −2 and 2 are not included.

−2<x<2

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

(−2,2)

More formally, we can also write

x∈(−2,2).

question.html:
Question 1
?

The inequality −2<x<2 can be expressed in interval notation as

a
(−2,2)
b
[−2,2]
c
(−2,2]
d
[−2,2)
e
(−∞,2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints −2 and 2 are not included.

−2<x<2

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

(−2,2)

More formally, we can also write

x∈(−2,2).

(-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2})

x\in (-\sqrt{2},\sqrt{2}).
$$

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Converting Between Intervals and Inequalities: Open Intervals
last_observation.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints $-3$ and $-1$ are *not* included. 

$$
-3\,\,<\,\,x\,\,<\,\,-1
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
(-3,-1)
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in (-3,-1).
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

The inequality −3<x<−1 can be expressed in interval notation as

a
[−3,−1]
b
(−3,−1)
c
(1,3)
d
[−3,−1)
e
(−3,−1]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

Our inequality contains only "less than" symbols. So, the endpoints −3 and −1 are not included.

−3<x<−1

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

(−3,−1)

More formally, we can also write

x∈(−3,−1).

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Which inequality corresponds to the interval $x\in [-7,0]?$
question.worked_solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $(,)$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

Our interval contains only brackets. So, the endpoints *are* included. 

$$
x\in [-7,0]
$$

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

$$
-7\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,\le \,\,0
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Which inequality corresponds to the interval x∈[−7,0]?

a
−7<x≤0
b
−7≤x<0
c
x≤−7 or x≥0
d
−7<x<0
e
−7≤x≤0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (0,0) to indicate that the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] to indicate that the endpoints are included.

Our interval contains only brackets. So, the endpoints are included.

x∈[−7,0]

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

−7≤x≤0

Question 3
?

Which inequality corresponds to the interval x∈[−7,0]?

a
−7<x≤0
b
−7≤x<0
c
x≤−7 or x≥0
d
−7<x<0
e
−7≤x≤0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (0,0) to indicate that the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] to indicate that the endpoints are included.

Our interval contains only brackets. So, the endpoints are included.

x∈[−7,0]

Therefore, our interval can be expressed as the following inequality:

−7≤x≤0

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: The inequality $-10\le x\le 3$ can be expressed in interval notation as
question.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints $-10$ and $3$ *are* included. 

$$
-10\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,\le \,\,3
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
[-10,3]
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in [-10,3].
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

The inequality −10≤x≤3 can be expressed in interval notation as

a
[−10,3)
b
(−10,3]
c
[−10,3]
d
(−∞,3]
e
(−10,3)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints −10 and 3 are included.

−10≤x≤3

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

[−10,3]

More formally, we can also write

x∈[−10,3].

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: The inequality $-10\le x\le 3$ can be expressed in interval notation as
feedback.worked_solution:
Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ if the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ if the endpoints *are* included.

Our inequality contains only "or equal to" symbols. So, the endpoints $-10$ and $3$ *are* included. 

$$
-10\,\,\le \,\,x\,\,\le \,\,3
$$

Therefore, we can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

$$
[-10,3]
$$

More formally, we can also write

$$
x\in [-10,3].
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: The interval $y\in [-1,2)$ corresponds to the inequality
question.worked_solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

For the given interval 

$$
[-1,2\,)
$$

we note the following:

- The left endpoint $-1$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $\le \,.$

- The right endpoint $2$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $<\,.$

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
-1\,\,\le \,\,y\,\,<\,\,2.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The interval y∈[−1,2) corresponds to the inequality

a
−1<y<2
b
−1<y≤2
c
−2<y≤1
d
−1≤y<2
e
−1≤y≤2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) to indicate that the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] to indicate that the endpoints are included.

For the given interval

[−1,2)

we note the following:

  • The left endpoint −1 is included in the interval. Therefore, we use ≤.

  • The right endpoint 2 is not included in the interval. Therefore, we use <.

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is −1≤y<2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

- Parentheses $()$ to indicate that the endpoints are *not* included.

- Brackets $[]$ to indicate that the endpoints *are* included.

For the given interval 

$$
[-1,2\,)
$$

we note the following:

- The left endpoint $-1$ *is* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $\le \,.$

- The right endpoint $2$ is *not* included in the interval. Therefore, we use $<\,.$

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is 

$$
-1\,\,\le \,\,y\,\,<\,\,2.
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

The interval y∈[−1,2) corresponds to the inequality

a
−1<y<2
b
−1<y≤2
c
−2<y≤1
d
−1≤y<2
e
−1≤y≤2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every interval can be expressed as an inequality. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) to indicate that the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] to indicate that the endpoints are included.

For the given interval

[−1,2)

we note the following:

  • The left endpoint −1 is included in the interval. Therefore, we use ≤.

  • The right endpoint 2 is not included in the interval. Therefore, we use <.

Therefore, the inequality that corresponds to the given interval is −1≤y<2.

question.html:
Question 6
?

The inequality −5≤x<−2 can be expressed in interval notation as

a
x∈[−5,−2]
b
x∈(−5,−2)
c
x∈[−5,−2)
d
x∈(−5,−2]
e
x∈[−5,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

For the given inequality

−5≤x<−2

we note the following:

  • The left endpoint −5 is included in the interval. Therefore, we use [.

  • The right endpoint −2 is not included in the interval. Therefore, we use ).

Therefore, the corresponding interval is

x∈[−5,−2).

question.html:
Question 6
?

The inequality −5≤x<−2 can be expressed in interval notation as

a
x∈[−5,−2]
b
x∈(−5,−2)
c
x∈[−5,−2)
d
x∈(−5,−2]
e
x∈[−5,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

For the given inequality

−5≤x<−2

we note the following:

  • The left endpoint −5 is included in the interval. Therefore, we use [.

  • The right endpoint −2 is not included in the interval. Therefore, we use ).

Therefore, the corresponding interval is

x∈[−5,−2).
question.knowledge_point: Translating Between Half-Open Intervals and Inequalities

solution.reasoning: The inequality includes -5 and excludes -2, so use a bracket at -5 and a parenthesis at -2: x\in [-5,-2), option c. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

question.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following intervals corresponds to the segment shown above?

a
 x∈[2,4]
b
x∈(2,4)
c
x∈(2,4]
d
x∈[2,4)
e
x∈[2,∞)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Every inequality can be expressed as an interval. We use the following notations:

  • Parentheses (00) if the endpoints are not included.

  • Brackets [00] if the endpoints are included.

The given interval can be represented by the following inequality:

2≤x<4

We can express our inequality in interval notation as follows:

x∈[2,4)

solution.reasoning: The segment runs from 2 to 4, with a filled circle at 2 and an open circle at 4. Thus 2 is included and 4 is excluded, giving x\in [2,4), option d. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question was captured.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\operatorname{sin}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡z.$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={tan}^{2}⁡(3x-5y).
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=3x-5y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-5y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-5\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{5}-\frac{1}{5}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={tan}^{2}⁡z\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-5{tan}^{2}⁡z.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=3-5{tan}^{2}⁡z.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x+2y+5}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=x+2y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2} & ={e}^{z+5}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{z+5}+1.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2{e}^{z+5}+1.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{1}{(3x-y)^{3}}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=3x-y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=3x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =3-\frac{1}{{z}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{z}^{3}}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=\frac{1}{{z}^{3}}.$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=(2x-3y)^{2}.
$$

Using a substitution of the form $z=2x-3y,$ transform the differential equation into an equation of the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z).$ What is the function $f(z)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=2x-3y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-3\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & ={z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z),$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=2-3{z}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, $f(z)=2-3{z}^{2}.$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{{e}^{y-x}}{x-y+1}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=x+C,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x-y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-\frac{{e}^{-z}}{z+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{-z}}{z+1}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(z+1){e}^{z}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int (z+1){e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z+1 & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{z} & \,⟹\,v={e}^{z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (z+1){e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ (z+1){e}^{z}-\int {e}^{z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \text{d}x \\ (z+1){e}^{z}-{e}^{z} & =x+C \\ z{e}^{z} & =x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
(x-y){e}^{x-y}=x+C
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=(x-y){e}^{x-y}.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{x+y}-x-y}{x+y}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{{e}^{z}-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{z}}{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{{e}^{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-z} & \,⟹\,v=-{e}^{-z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}+\int {e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}-{e}^{-z} & =x+C \\ -{e}^{-z}(z+1) & =x+K \\ {e}^{-z}(z+1) & =C-x\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
{e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1)=C-x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1).$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y)}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-2x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+2y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+2\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}-\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡z}{2}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \frac{1}{2}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡z\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡z & =x+K \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡z & =C-2x,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-2K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y)=C-2x\,\,
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y).$
