questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}(-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(1-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4(3t-1)+9(1-t) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3t+5 \\ 23-15t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 \\ -6 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}+\,\,\frac{1}{9}$ {{field-1}} .
$39t+23$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{t}-{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =4t\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int (-{e}^{-t})\cdot (-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{-t}-\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{-t}+{e}^{-t} \\  & ={e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4(3t-1)+9(t+1) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}21t+5 \\ 39t+23\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+\,\,\frac{1}{4}$ $36t-42$ .

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-2t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}6t \\ 3t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot 3{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -3{e}^{-2t} & 2{e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -{e}^{2t} \\ -3{e}^{t} & 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6t \\ 3t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3t{e}^{2t} \\ 12t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-3t{e}^{2t} \\ 12t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -3t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 12t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=-3t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-3\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -3t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(-3t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}\cdot (-3\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{3}{2}\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}t{e}^{2t}+\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=12t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=12\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 12t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =12t\cdot {e}^{t}-\int 12\cdot {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12t{e}^{t}-12{e}^{t} \\  & =12{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t} \\ 3{e}^{-2t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{4}{e}^{2t}(1-2t) \\ 12{e}^{t}(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}6(1-2t)+48(t-1) \\ 9(1-2t)+48(t-1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}36t-42 \\ 30t-39\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 5{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot {e}^{t}-5{e}^{t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -5{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{4{e}^{-2t}}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -5{e}^{t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -5{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =-\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -5{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{-t} & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 2t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t} \\ -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t} \\ -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=\frac{5}{2}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\frac{5}{2}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{5}{2}t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(\frac{5}{2}t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (\frac{5}{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{5}{6}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{5}{6}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{5}{6}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{5}{18}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{5}{18}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-\frac{1}{2}t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-{e}^{-t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t & =(-\frac{1}{2}t)\cdot (-{e}^{-t})-\int -{e}^{-t}\cdot (-\frac{1}{2}\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}-\frac{1}{2}\int {e}^{-t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{2}t{e}^{-t}+\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & 5{e}^{t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{18}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{-t}(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}5(3t-1)+45(t+1) \\ 5(3t-1)+9(t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}30t+20 \\ 12t+2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]x(t)+[\begin{aligned}5t \\ t\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations. Using the method of variation of parameters, the general solution of the equation can be written in the form
$x(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}+\,\,\frac{1}{9}$ {{field-1}} .

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{3t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}5t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =4t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t} \\  & =4{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=\,\text{d}t$ and $v=-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}36(t-1)-(3t+1) \\ -(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}33t-37 \\ -3t-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form $\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \mathbf{u}(t),$ where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for $\mathbf x_p(t)$ is given below. 

$\textrm{L1}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \mathbf{u}(t)$

$\textrm{L2}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{x}'_p(t) = \Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) + \Phi' \mathbf{u}(t)$

$\textrm{L3}{:}\:$ $\Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) + \Phi' \mathbf{u}(t) = A \Phi \mathbf{u}(t) + \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L4}{:}\:$ $\Phi' = A \Phi$

$\textrm{L5}{:}\:$ $\Phi \mathbf{u}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L6}{:}\:$ $\mathbf{u}'(t) = \Phi^{-1}(t) \mathbf{f}(t)$

$\textrm{L7}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t$

$\textrm{L8}{:}\:$ $\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t$

Fill in the blanks with the correct reasons to justify each step of the reasoning.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L4}$ follows from the fact that ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/e2e16ba2ee71f82214649c533dc658cdba72e3b3f49cf8563f117ee2fe89a07d.svg) matrix.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L6}$ follows from line $\textrm{L5}$ by  ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/2dd0b78f14b4f044b6c747da364728bb5555f5c36710b6bf66ab74cc7f5e294f.svg) both sides of the equation.

$\quad$ Line $\textrm{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\textrm{L7}$ into ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/01ab649cd1dec87ec0dd5c1f3f8f79ce76553d52463ae2c6102c0ce7be67163d.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\textrm{L4}.$ Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system $\mathbf{x}'(t) =A\mathbf{x}(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $\mathbf{c}(t)$ of $\Phi$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
\mathbf{c}'(t) =A\mathbf{c}(t),
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Particular Solution of an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/02f22b5daa1290af87e8a15340bd2e75abdb9305136f9b7f3162763e4dee440e.svg)
Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute $\Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t)$ and the particular solution $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ of the system.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/3139ce9adc8c4803bc8cf3332e76c2bad4cb35489024478178ab74023dee7e44.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_c(t) + \mathbf{x}_p(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_c(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/8570eb051b14077d86cbe0cda29f79d12de8529001c6e9b3a2698c107792ef1b.svg)

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/9fe602a563fbfbfd3f3331df7243ebf1aa5aa1c90a01550a033d4a4dfd0f0639.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 0\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=2t$ and $\text{d}v=e^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, the integrand is zero, so the integral is zero.

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Consider the system of ordinary differential equations

$$
\mathbf{x}'(t) =
A
\mathbf{x}(t) +
\mathbf{f}(t)
$$

where $A$ is a constant square matrix and $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is a forcing vector.

In this lesson, we'll derive the formula for the particular solution of the above system using the method of variation of parameters.

Recall that the general solution of the corresponding homogeneous system is given by

$$
\mathbf{x}_c(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{c}
$$

where $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector of constants, and $\Phi$ is the fundamental matrix.

As usual, for the method of variation of parameters, we'll look for a particular solution of our inhomogeneous system by varying the constant parameters, i.e., in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{u}(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined.

Differentiating $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ with respect to $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φ\,u(t))^{′} \\  & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a solution, substituting it back into the initial system gives a true equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, $\Phi' = A \Phi.$ Substituting this into the equation simplifies it to the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+AΦu(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t) & =f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, since $\Phi$ is invertible, we can pre-multiply both sides by $\Phi^{-1}{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate both sides of the final equations (ignoring the constant term):

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t) = \Phi \displaystyle\int \Phi^{-1}\mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

question.html:
Question 1
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L4 follows from the fact that
A is the identity
A is the identity
Φ is a square
Φ is a fundamental
A is an invertible
matrix.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
integrating
adding Φ to
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating
adding Φ to
differentiating
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
both sides of the equation.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider line L4. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), i.e., by substituting any column c(t) of Φ into the homogeneous system, we get c′(t)=Ac(t), where c′(t) is the corresponding column of derivatives in Φ. As a result, this means that Φ′=AΦ. Therefore, L4 follows from the fact that Φ is a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} .

Question 2
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)

  • Next, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

  • Finally, we consider lines L1, L7, and L8. Substituting u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt from L7 into L1, we get xp(t)=Φu(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt. Therefore, L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into L1.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}.

Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

Question 3

Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L2 follows from line L1 by
integrating

adding Φ to
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating

EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

  • Finally, we consider lines L1, L7, and L8. Substituting u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt from L7 into L1, we get xp(t)=Φu(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt. Therefore, L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into L1.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-3}} .
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), i.e., by substituting any column c(t) of Φ into the homogeneous system, we get c′(t)=Ac(t), where c′(t) is the corresponding column of derivatives in Φ. As a result, this means that Φ′=AΦ. Therefore, L4 follows from the fact that Φ is a fundamental matrix.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/462d34097bc5fc13a20c3dc46426c9c0e202895f3d419690102b29c24fc221d6.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/462d34097bc5fc13a20c3dc46426c9c0e202895f3d419690102b29c24fc221d6.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{0\cdot (-2{e}^{-4t})-2{e}^{-4t}\cdot {e}^{3t}}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}-2{e}^{-4t} & -2{e}^{-4t} \\ -{e}^{3t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{4t} & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} \\ 2{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 3{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{5t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2{e}^{-4t} \\ {e}^{3t} & -2{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}{e}^{-2t} \\ \frac{1}{10}{e}^{5t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}{e}^{t} \\ -\frac{17}{10}{e}^{t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{t}[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{17}{10}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{x}_c(t) + \mathbf{x}_p(t)
$$

where $\mathbf{x}_c(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and $\mathbf{x}_p(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/0969f57a73d9be0faf4cc11b8edbf60b4f163385a9ef6de2ed7cd3799944ab7f.svg)

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
\mathbf{x}_p(t)  = \Phi \, \mathbf{u}(t)
$$

where $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $\mathbf{f}(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
\mathbf{u}(t) = \int \Phi^{-1} \, \mathbf{f}(t) \, \text{d}t.
$$

In our case,
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14159277/assets/3e6801be0a59a55dd651f97f1b796bff8432688a9e0dd8eb0d1f99a02792876e.svg)

Since $\Phi$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2 \times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-2t}\cdot {e}^{-4t}-0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{6t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-4t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}]. \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2t \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $\mathbf{u}(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}2t{e}^{2t} \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int 0\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=2t$ and $\text{d}v=e^{2t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\dfrac{1}{2}e^{2t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2t{e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t & =(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}-\int \frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2\,\text{d}t) \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\int {e}^{2t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =t{e}^{2t}-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, the integrand is zero, so the integral is zero.

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-2t} & 0 \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2t}(2t-1) \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2t-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 11
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Solving an Inhomogeneous System of Linear ODEs Using Variation of Parameters
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

- For the second component, let $u=-t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=-\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(-t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}(-\,\text{d}t) \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+\int {e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-t{e}^{t}+{e}^{t} \\  & ={e}^{t}(1-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1) \\ {e}^{t}(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}4(3t-1)+9(1-t) \\ 4(3t-1)+27(1-t)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}3t+5 \\ 23-15t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.

In our case,

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{3t}-{e}^{3t}\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={e}^{-2t}[\begin{aligned}{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{t} & -{e}^{t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{t} \\ t{e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v={e}^{t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot {e}^{t}-\int {e}^{t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =4t{e}^{t}-4{e}^{t} \\  & =4{e}^{t}(t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}

$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L4 follows from the fact that
A is the identity
A is the identity
Φ is a square
Φ is a fundamental
A is an invertible
matrix.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
differentiating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
integrating
adding Φ to
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating
adding Φ to
differentiating
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
both sides of the equation.
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider line L4. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), i.e., by substituting any column c(t) of Φ into the homogeneous system, we get c′(t)=Ac(t), where c′(t) is the corresponding column of derivatives in Φ. As a result, this means that Φ′=AΦ. Therefore, L4 follows from the fact that Φ is a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$

$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} .

Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.html:
Question 2
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the
initial system of ODEs
first shifting theorem
line L4
initial system of ODEs
solution of the system of ODEs
.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
adding Φ to
differentiating
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
adding Φ
integrating
differentiating
both sides of the equation.

Line L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into
L1
L3
L2
L1
L6
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)

  • Next, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

  • Finally, we consider lines L1, L7, and L8. Substituting u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt from L7 into L1, we get xp(t)=Φu(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt. Therefore, L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into L1.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} .

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-1}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-4}} .
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into $\text{initial system of ODEs}.$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$
