last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Constructing the Formulas for Variation of Parameters
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}.
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

  • Finally, we consider lines L1, L7, and L8. Substituting u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt from L7 into L1, we get xp(t)=Φu(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt. Therefore, L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into L1.

feedback.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-2}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting {{field-3}} into {{field-4}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1}.$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L2 follows from line L1 by
differentiating
integrating
differentiating
adding Φ to
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
both sides of the equation.

Line L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the
initial system of ODEs
initial system of ODEs
solution of the system of ODEs
line L4
first shifting theorem
.

Line L6 follows from line L5 by
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
adding Φ
differentiating
integrating
both sides of the equation.

Line L7 follows from line L6 by
integrating
adding Φ to
differentiating
pre-multiplying by Φ−1
integrating
both sides of the equation.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next we consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t).

  • Finally, we consider lines L6 and L7. To get L7, we are integrating both sides of the equation in L6: ∫u′(t)dt=∫Φ−1(t)f(t)dtu(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation.
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$

Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

differentiating

pre-multiplying by Φ−1
both sides of the equation.

EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider lines L1 and L2. To get L2, we are differentiating with respect to t both sides of the equation in L1: xp′(t)=(Φu(t))′xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

  • Next we consider lines L1, L2, and L3. Let's substitute xp(t)=Φu(t) from L1 and xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t) from L2 into the initial system of ODEs: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) Therefore, L3 is obtained by substituting L1 and L2 into the initial system of ODEs.

  • Next, we consider lines L5 and L6. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, Φ is invertible. Therefore, L6 follows from L5 by pre-multiplying by Φ−1 both sides of the equation: Φ−1⋅Φu′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)(Φ−1Φ)⋅u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t)u′(t)=Φ−1⋅f(t).

feedback.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L2}$ follows from line $\text{L1}$ by {{field-1}} both sides of  the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}$ into the {{field-2}}.

$\,$ Line $\text{L6}$ follows from line $\text{L5}$ by {{field-3}} both sides of the equation.

$\,$ Line $\text{L7}$ follows from line $\text{L6}$ by {{field-4}} both sides of the equation.
feedback.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider lines $\text{L1}$ and $\text{L2}.$ To get $\text{L2},$ we are $\text{differentiating}$ with respect to $t$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L1}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =(Φu(t))^{′} \\ {x}_{p}^{′}(t) & =Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)\end{aligned}
$$

- Next we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L2},$ and $\text{L3}.$ Let's substitute ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$ from $\text{L1}$ and ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$ from $\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) & =Ax(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t) & =AΦu(t)+f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L3}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L1}\text{ and }\text{L2}$ into the initial system of ODEs.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L5}$ and $\text{L6}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are linearly independent. So, $Φ$ is invertible. Therefore, $\text{L6}$ follows from $\text{L5}$ by $\text{pre-multiplying by }{Φ}^{-1}$ both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\cdot Φ{u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ ({Φ}^{-1}Φ)\cdot {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t) \\ {u}^{′}(t) & ={Φ}^{-1}\cdot f(t).\end{aligned}
$$

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L6}$ and $\text{L7}.$ To get $\text{L7},$ we are $\text{integrating}$ both sides of the equation in $\text{L6}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {u}^{′}(t)\,\text{d}t & =\int {Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)\,\text{d}t \\ u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-3}} .
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.html:
Question 5
?
Consider the following system of differential equations: x′(t)=Ax(t)+f(t) Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form xp(t)=Φu(t), where Φ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and u(t) is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for xp(t) is given below.

L1: xp(t)=Φu(t)

L2: xp′(t)=Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)

L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)

L4: Φ′=AΦ

L5: Φu′(t)=f(t)

L6: u′(t)=Φ−1(t)f(t)

L7: u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt

L8: xp(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

Line L4 follows from the fact that
Φ is a fundamental
Φ is a fundamental
Φ is a square
A is an invertible
A is the identity
matrix.

Line L5 follows from lines
L3 and L4
L3 and L4
L2 and L4
L1 and L4
L2 and L3
by substitution.

Line L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into
L1
L3
L6
L2
L1
.
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let's examine each statement in turn.

  • We first consider line L4. Since Φ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system x′(t)=Ax(t), i.e., by substituting any column c(t) of Φ into the homogeneous system, we get c′(t)=Ac(t), where c′(t) is the corresponding column of derivatives in Φ. As a result, this means that Φ′=AΦ. Therefore, L4 follows from the fact that Φ is a fundamental matrix.

  • Next, we consider lines L3, L4, and L5. Let's substitute Φ′=AΦ from L4 into L3: Φu′(t)+Φ′u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)+AΦu(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)Φu′(t)=f(t) Therefore, L5 follows from L3 and L4 by substitution.

  • Finally, we consider lines L1, L7, and L8. Substituting u(t)=∫Φ−1f(t)dt from L7 into L1, we get xp(t)=Φu(t)=Φ∫Φ−1f(t)dt. Therefore, L8 is obtained by substituting L7 into L1.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following system of differential equations:

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t)+f(t)
$$

Using the method of variation of parameters, we wish to find a particular solution in the form ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t),$ where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system and $u(t)$ is a column vector of functions to be determined. A derivation of the formula for ${x}_{p}(t)$ is given below. 

$\text{L1}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φu(t)$

$\text{L2}:\,$ ${x}_{p}^{′}(t)=Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)$

$\text{L3}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t)$

$\text{L4}:\,$ ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$

$\text{L5}:\,$ $Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)$

$\text{L6}:\,$ ${u}^{′}(t)={Φ}^{-1}(t)f(t)$

$\text{L7}:\,$ $u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

$\text{L8}:\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t$

Select the correct options in the following reasoning.

$\,$ Line $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that {{field-1}} matrix.

$\,$ Line $\text{L5}$ follows from lines {{field-2}} by substitution.

$\,$ Line $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into {{field-3}} .
question.worked_solution:
Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

Let's examine each statement in turn.

- We first consider line $\text{L4}.$ Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, its columns are solutions to the homogeneous system ${x}^{′}(t)=Ax(t),$ i.e., by substituting any column $c(t)$ of $Φ$ into the homogeneous system, we get

$$
{c}^{′}(t)=Ac(t),
$$

where ${c}^{′}(t)$ is the corresponding column of derivatives in $Φ.$ As a result, this means that ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ.$ Therefore, $\text{L4}$ follows from the fact that $Φ\text{ is a fundamental}$ matrix.

- Next, we consider lines $\text{L3}$, $\text{L4},$ and $\text{L5}.$ Let's substitute ${Φ}^{′}=AΦ$ from $\text{L4}$ into $\text{L3}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Φ{u}^{′}(t)+{Φ}^{′}u(t)=AΦu(t)+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)+\cancel{AΦu(t)}=\cancel{AΦu(t)}+f(t) \\ Φ{u}^{′}(t)=f(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L5}$ follows from $\text{L3}\text{ and }\text{L4}$ by substitution.

- Finally, we consider lines $\text{L1},$ $\text{L7},$ and $\text{L8}.$ Substituting

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t
$$

from $\text{L7}$ into $\text{L1},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φu(t) \\  & =Φ\int {Φ}^{-1}f(t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{L8}$ is obtained by substituting $\text{L7}$ into  $\text{L1}.$

question.problem:
$$ {x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]x(t)+\overset{f(t)}{\overset{⏞}{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}]}},\,Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}] $$ Consider the system of differential equations and the fundamental matrix of the corresponding homogeneous system above. Using the method of variation of parameters, compute ${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)$ and the particular solution ${x}_{p}(t)$ of the system.
${Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)=\,\,$ $-10{e}^{-2t}$ $\,,\,$ ${x}_{p}(t)=\,\,$ $2$
{{field-1}} {{field-2}}
question.worked_solution:
We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{2t}\cdot 2{e}^{4t}-(-3{e}^{4t})\cdot 0}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{{e}^{-6t}}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{4t} & 3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & {e}^{2t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\ {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}2{e}^{-2t} & 3{e}^{-2t} \\ 0 & {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}-10{e}^{-2t} \\ -4{e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int -10{e}^{-2t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -4{e}^{-4t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{2t} & -3{e}^{4t} \\ 0 & 2{e}^{4t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5{e}^{-2t} \\ {e}^{-4t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that the general solution of an inhomogeneous system can be written as 

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)
$$

where ${x}_{c}(t)$ is the complementary solution (solution of the corresponding homogeneous system) and ${x}_{p}(t)$ is a particular solution.

Notice that we are given that

$$
{x}_{c}(t)={c}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]{e}^{-3t}+{c}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]{e}^{-t}.
$$

We'll look for a particular solution in the form

$$
{x}_{p}(t)=Φ\,u(t)
$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.
$$

In our case,

$$
Φ=[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-t} \\ {e}^{-3t} & 3{e}^{-t}\end{aligned}],\,f(t)=[\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}].
$$

Since $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix, it must be invertible. Using the formula for the inverse of a $2\times 2$ matrix, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1} & =\frac{1}{{e}^{-3t}\cdot 3{e}^{-t}-{e}^{-t}\cdot {e}^{-3t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2{e}^{-4t}}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{-t} & -{e}^{-t} \\ -{e}^{-3t} & {e}^{-3t}\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{Φ}^{-1}\,f(t) & =\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}3{e}^{3t} & -{e}^{3t} \\ -{e}^{t} & {e}^{t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3t \\ t\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using our formula for $u(t),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}u(t) & =\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int [\begin{aligned}4t{e}^{3t} \\ -t{e}^{t}\end{aligned}]\,\text{d}t \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\ \int -t{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Integrating the components by parts, we get the following:

- For the first component, let $u=4t$ and $\text{d}v={e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t.$ Then, $\text{d}u=4\,\text{d}t$ and $v=\frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4t{e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t & =(4t)\cdot \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}-\int \frac{1}{3}{e}^{3t}\cdot (4\,\text{d}t) \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{3}\int {e}^{3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{4}{3}t{e}^{3t}-\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t} \\  & =\frac{4}{9}{e}^{3t}(3t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

where $Φ$ is a fundamental matrix for the corresponding homogeneous system, $f(t)$ is the forcing column vector and

$$
u(t)=\int {Φ}^{-1}\,f(t)\,\text{d}t.

$$
x(t)={x}_{c}(t)+{x}_{p}(t)

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}\int t{e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t & =t\cdot (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})-\int (-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3t})\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}+\frac{1}{3}\int {e}^{-3t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =-\frac{t}{3}{e}^{-3t}-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t} \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our particular solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{p}(t) & =Φ\,u(t) \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{e}^{-t} & {e}^{3t} \\ 0 & {e}^{3t}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4{e}^{t}(t-1) \\ -\frac{1}{9}{e}^{-3t}(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}36(t-1)-(3t+1) \\ -(3t+1)\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}[\begin{aligned}33t-37 \\ -3t-1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
6{w}^{2}+19w+10.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($6\times 10=60$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($19$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $60.$

The positive factor pairs of $60$ are

$$
(1,60),\,(2,30),\,(3,10),\,(4,15),\,(5,12),\,(6,10).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(4,15)$ add to $19:$ 

$$
4+15=19\,✓
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $4w+15w,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{w}^{2}+19w+10 & = \\ 6{w}^{2}+4w+15w+10 & = \\ (6{w}^{2}+4w)+(15w+10) & = \\ 2w(3w+2)+5(3w+2) & = \\ (3w+2)(2w+5)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
10{m}^{2}+13m+4.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10\times 4=40$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($13$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $40.$

The positive factor pairs of $40$ are

$$
(1,40),\,(2,20),\,(4,10),\,(5,8).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,8)$ add to $13:$ 

$$
5+8=13\,✓
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5m+8m,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{m}^{2}+13m+4 & = \\ 10{m}^{2}+5m+8m+4 & = \\ (10{m}^{2}+5m)+(8m+4) & = \\ 5m(2m+1)+4(2m+1) & = \\ (5m+4)(2m+1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
5{b}^{2}-34b-7.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($5\times -7=-35$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-34$).

First, we find the factor pairs of $-35:$

$$
(1,-35),\,(-1,35),\,(5,-7),\,(-5,7)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(1,-35)$ add to $-34:$ 

$$
1+(-35)=-34\,✓
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $b-35b,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{b}^{2}-34b-7 & = \\ 5{b}^{2}+b-35b-7 & = \\ (5{b}^{2}+b)-(35b+7) & = \\ b(5b+1)-7(5b+1) & = \\ (b-7)(5b+1) & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
5{h}^{2}-12h-9.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($5\times -9=-45$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-12$).

The factor pairs of $-45$ are

$$
(1,-45),\,\,(-1,45),\,\,(3,-15),\,\,(-3,15),\,\,(5,-9),\,\,(-5,9).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(3,-15)$ add to $-12:$ 

$$
3-15=-12\,✓
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $3h-15h,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{h}^{2}-12h-9 & = \\ 5{h}^{2}+3h-15h-9 & = \\ 5{h}^{2}-15h+3h-9 & = \\ (5{h}^{2}-15h)+(3h-9) & = \\ 5h(h-3)+3(h-3) & = \\ (5h+3)(h-3) & \end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
4{x}^{2}-15x+9.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($4\times 9=36$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-15$).

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we only need to consider the negative factor pairs of $36.$

The negative factor pairs of $36$ are

$$
(-1,-36),\,(-2,-18),\,(-3,-12),\,(-4,-9),\,(-6,-6).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-3,-12)$ add to $-15:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}(-3)+(-12) & =-15\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-3x-12x,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}-15x+9 & = \\ 4{x}^{2}-3x-12x+9 & = \\ (4{x}^{2}-3x)-(12x-9) & = \\ x(4x-3)-3(4x-3) & = \\ (x-3)(4x-3) & \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Factor the quadratic expression $10a^2 + 11a + 3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
10a^2 + 11a + 3.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10 \times 3 = 30$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($11$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $30.$

The positive factor pairs of $30$ are

$$
(1,30), \quad (2,15), \quad (3,10), \quad (5,6).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,6)$ add to $11{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5+6 & =11\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5a + 6a,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{a}^{2}+11a+3 & = \\ 10{a}^{2}+5a+6a+3 & = \\ (10{a}^{2}+5a)+(6a+3) & = \\ 5a(2a+1)+3(2a+1) & = \\ (5a+3)(2a+1) & \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Factor the quadratic expression $2c^2 + 15c - 8.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
2c^2 + 15c - 8.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times -8 = -16$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($15$).

First, we find the factor pairs of $-16{:}$

$$
(1,-16),\quad (-1,16), \quad (2,-8), \quad (-2,8), \quad (4,-4)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,16)$ add to $15{:}$ 

$$
(-1) + 16 = 15 \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $- c+16c,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{c}^{2}+15c-8 & = \\ 2{c}^{2}-c+16c-8 & = \\ (2{c}^{2}-c)+(16c-8) & = \\ c(2c-1)+8(2c-1) & = \\ (2c-1)(c+8) & \end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
3x^2 - 16x + 16.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($3 \times 16 = 48$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-16$).

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we only need to consider the negative factor pairs of $48.$

The negative factor pairs of $48$ are

$$
(-1,-48), \quad (-2,-24), \quad (-3,-16), \quad (-4,-12), \quad (-6,-8).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-4,-12)$ add to $-16{:}$ 

$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
In a previous lesson, we learned how to factor quadratic trinomials whose quadratic coefficient equals one. In this lesson, we'll extend our understanding to include cases where the quadratic coefficient is a positive integer that's different from one.

For example, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}x^2+{\color{purple}{7}}x+{\color{blue}{3}}
$$

 

Notice that the quadratic coefficient equals ${\color{red}{2}}.$

To factor this trinomial, we must find two numbers that 

- *multiply* to give the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant $({\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6),$ and

- *add* to give the linear coefficient $({\color{purple}{7}})$.

We can factor this trinomial in four steps:

- **Step 1:**  We start by writing down the factor pairs of $6{:}$

The factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(1,6), \qquad (2,3).
$$

- **Step 2:**  Determine which of these factor pairs add up to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{7}})\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}1+6 & =7 & ✓ \\ 2+3 & =5 & \times \end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 3:**  Using the factor pair identified in the previous step, write the linear term as $7x=x+6x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+7x+3 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+x+6x+3\end{aligned}
$$

- **Step 4:**  Factor the first two terms and the last two terms separately and then factor the expression completely:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}+x+6x+3 & = \\ x(2x+1)+3(2x+1) & = \\ (2x+1)(x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

And we're done! 

We can check that our answer is correct by expanding the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(2x+1)(x+3) & = \\ 2x\cdot (x+3)+1\cdot (x+3) & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+6x+x+3 & = \\ 2{x}^{2}+7x+3 & \,✓\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants
tutorials.problem:
To factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant that adds to the linear coefficient.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}y^2 {\color{purple}{\,-\,7}}y + {\color{blue}{3}}
$$

Notice that,

- the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant, ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6$, is *positive*, while

- the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}})$ is *negative*.

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $6.$

The negative factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(-1,-6), \quad (-2,-3).
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their sum is *negative*, which is what we want.

Now, we determine which of these factor pairs sums to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)+(-6) & =-7\,✓ \\ (-2)+(-3) & =-5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-y - 6y,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-7y+3 & = \\ 2{y}^{2}-y-6y+3 & = \\ (2{y}^{2}-y)-(6y-3) & = \\ y(2y-1)-3(2y-1) & = \\ (y-3)(2y-1) & \end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
10a^2 + 11a + 3.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10 \times 3 = 30$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($11$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $30.$

The positive factor pairs of $30$ are

$$
(1,30), \quad (2,15), \quad (3,10), \quad (5,6).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,6)$ add to $11{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}5+6 & =11\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5a + 6a,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{a}^{2}+11a+3 & = \\ 10{a}^{2}+5a+6a+3 & = \\ (10{a}^{2}+5a)+(6a+3) & = \\ 5a(2a+1)+3(2a+1) & = \\ (5a+3)(2a+1) & \end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
6{w}^{2}+19w+10.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($6\times 10=60$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($19$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $60.$

The positive factor pairs of $60$ are

$$
(1,60),\,(2,30),\,(3,10),\,(4,15),\,(5,12),\,(6,10).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(4,15)$ add to $19:$ 

$$
4+15=19\,✓
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $4w+15w,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{w}^{2}+19w+10 & = \\ 6{w}^{2}+4w+15w+10 & = \\ (6{w}^{2}+4w)+(15w+10) & = \\ 2w(3w+2)+5(3w+2) & = \\ (3w+2)(2w+5)\end{aligned}
$$

6w2+19w+10=

a
(3w+2)(2w+5)
b
(6w+1)(w+10)
c
(3w+10)(2w+1)
d
 (3w+5)(2w+2)
e
2(3w+1)(w+5)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must factor the quadratic expression 6w2+19w+10.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (6×10=60), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (19).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of 60.

The positive factor pairs of 60 are

(1,60),(2,30),(3,10),(4,15),(5,12),(6,10).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair (4,15) add to 19:

4+15=19✓

Then, we write the linear term as 4w+15w, and factor the result by grouping: 6w2+19w+10=6w2+4w+15w+10=(6w2+4w)+(15w+10)=2w(3w+2)+5(3w+2)=(3w+2)(2w+5)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
10{m}^{2}+13m+4.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10\times 4=40$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($13$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $40.$

The positive factor pairs of $40$ are

$$
(1,40),\,(2,20),\,(4,10),\,(5,8).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,8)$ add to $13:$ 

$$
5+8=13\,✓
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5m+8m,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{m}^{2}+13m+4 & = \\ 10{m}^{2}+5m+8m+4 & = \\ (10{m}^{2}+5m)+(8m+4) & = \\ 5m(2m+1)+4(2m+1) & = \\ (5m+4)(2m+1)\end{aligned}
$$

We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
2c^2 + 15c - 8.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($2 \times -8 = -16$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($15$).

First, we find the factor pairs of $-16{:}$

$$
(1,-16),\quad (-1,16), \quad (2,-8), \quad (-2,8), \quad (4,-4)
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(-1,16)$ add to $15{:}$ 

$$
(-1) + 16 = 15 \quad {\color{green}\checkmark}
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $- c+16c,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{c}^{2}+15c-8 & = \\ 2{c}^{2}-c+16c-8 & = \\ (2{c}^{2}-c)+(16c-8) & = \\ c(2c-1)+8(2c-1) & = \\ (2c-1)(c+8) & \end{aligned}
$$

We must factor the quadratic expression 5h2−12h−9.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (5×−9=−45), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (−12).

The factor pairs of −45 are

tutorial.name: Trinomials With Negative Linear Coefficients and Positive Constants
tutorial.problem:
To factor a quadratic expression, we must find a factor pair of the *product* of the quadratic coefficient and the constant that adds to the linear coefficient.

With that in mind, let's factor the following trinomial:

$$
{\color{red}{2}}y^2 {\color{purple}{\,-\,7}}y + {\color{blue}{3}}
$$

Notice that,

- the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant, ${\color{red}{2}} \times {\color{blue}{3}} = 6$, is *positive*, while

- the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}})$ is *negative*.

Since the linear coefficient is negative and the product of the quadratic coefficient and constant is positive, we need to consider the *negative* factor pairs of $6.$

The negative factor pairs of $6$ are

$$
(-1,-6), \quad (-2,-3).
$$

For each pair, their *product* is positive, and their sum is *negative*, which is what we want.

Now, we determine which of these factor pairs sums to the coefficient of the linear term $({\color{purple}{-7}}){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1)+(-6) & =-7\,✓ \\ (-2)+(-3) & =-5\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $-y - 6y,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{y}^{2}-7y+3 & = \\ 2{y}^{2}-y-6y+3 & = \\ (2{y}^{2}-y)-(6y-3) & = \\ y(2y-1)-3(2y-1) & = \\ (y-3)(2y-1) & \end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
6{w}^{2}+19w+10.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($6\times 10=60$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($19$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $60.$

The positive factor pairs of $60$ are

$$
(1,60),\,(2,30),\,(3,10),\,(4,15),\,(5,12),\,(6,10).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(4,15)$ add to $19:$ 

$$
4+15=19\,✓
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $4w+15w,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}6{w}^{2}+19w+10 & = \\ 6{w}^{2}+4w+15w+10 & = \\ (6{w}^{2}+4w)+(15w+10) & = \\ 2w(3w+2)+5(3w+2) & = \\ (3w+2)(2w+5)\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

6w2+19w+10=

a
(3w+2)(2w+5)
b
(6w+1)(w+10)
c
(3w+10)(2w+1)
d
 (3w+5)(2w+2)
e
2(3w+1)(w+5)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must factor the quadratic expression 6w2+19w+10.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (6×10=60), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (19).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of 60.

The positive factor pairs of 60 are

(1,60),(2,30),(3,10),(4,15),(5,12),(6,10).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair (4,15) add to 19:

4+15=19✓

Then, we write the linear term as 4w+15w, and factor the result by grouping: 6w2+19w+10=6w2+4w+15w+10=(6w2+4w)+(15w+10)=2w(3w+2)+5(3w+2)=(3w+2)(2w+5)

solution.reasoning: Expanding (3w+2)(2w+5) gives 6w^2+15w+4w+10=6w^2+19w+10, so option a is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different quadratic.

$$

$$

$$

$$
5+8=13\,✓

question.html:
Question 2
?

10m2+13m+4=

a
(5m+1)(m+4)
b
 (10m+1)(m+4)
c
2(5m+2)(m+1)
d
(5m+4)(2m+1)
e
2(5m+1)(m+2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must factor the quadratic expression 10m2+13m+4.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (10×4=40), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (13).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of 40.

The positive factor pairs of 40 are

(1,40),(2,20),(4,10),(5,8).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair (5,8) add to 13:

5+8=13✓

Then, we write the linear term as 5m+8m, and factor the result by grouping: 10m2+13m+4=10m2+5m+8m+4=(10m2+5m)+(8m+4)=5m(2m+1)+4(2m+1)=(5m+4)(2m+1)

question.html:
Question 2
?

10m2+13m+4=

a
(5m+1)(m+4)
b
 (10m+1)(m+4)
c
2(5m+2)(m+1)
d
(5m+4)(2m+1)
e
2(5m+1)(m+2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must factor the quadratic expression 10m2+13m+4.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (10×4=40), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (13).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of 40.

The positive factor pairs of 40 are

(1,40),(2,20),(4,10),(5,8).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair (5,8) add to 13:

5+8=13✓

Then, we write the linear term as 5m+8m, and factor the result by grouping: 10m2+13m+4=10m2+5m+8m+4=(10m2+5m)+(8m+4)=5m(2m+1)+4(2m+1)=(5m+4)(2m+1)
question.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomial With Positive Coefficients

solution.reasoning: Expanding (5m+4)(2m+1) gives 10m^2+5m+8m+4=10m^2+13m+4, so option d is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different quadratic.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
10{m}^{2}+13m+4.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($10\times 4=40$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($13$).

Since all coefficients are positive, we only need to consider the positive factor pairs of $40.$

The positive factor pairs of $40$ are

$$
(1,40),\,(2,20),\,(4,10),\,(5,8).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(5,8)$ add to $13:$ 

$$
5+8=13\,✓
$$

Then, we write the linear term as $5m+8m,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}10{m}^{2}+13m+4 & = \\ 10{m}^{2}+5m+8m+4 & = \\ (10{m}^{2}+5m)+(8m+4) & = \\ 5m(2m+1)+4(2m+1) & = \\ (5m+4)(2m+1)\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
5{h}^{2}-12h-9.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($5\times -9=-45$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-12$).

The factor pairs of $-45$ are

$$
(1,-45),\,\,(-1,45),\,\,(3,-15),\,\,(-3,15),\,\,(5,-9),\,\,(-5,9).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(3,-15)$ add to $-12:$ 

$$
3-15=-12\,✓
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $3h-15h,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{h}^{2}-12h-9 & = \\ 5{h}^{2}+3h-15h-9 & = \\ 5{h}^{2}-15h+3h-9 & = \\ (5{h}^{2}-15h)+(3h-9) & = \\ 5h(h-3)+3(h-3) & = \\ (5h+3)(h-3) & \end{aligned}
$$

We must factor the quadratic expression 5h2−12h−9.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (5×−9=−45), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (−12).

The factor pairs of −45 are

(1,−45),(−1,45),(3,−15),(−3,15),(5,−9),(−5,9).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair (3,−15) add to −12:

3−15=−12✓

5h2−12h−9=5h2+3h−15h−9=5h2−15h+3h−9=(5h2−15h)+(3h−9)=5h(h−3)+3(h−3)=(5h+3)(h−3)

last_observation.worked_solution:
We must factor the quadratic expression

$$
5{h}^{2}-12h-9.
$$

First, we find two numbers that 

- multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant ($5\times -9=-45$), and

- add to the linear coefficient ($-12$).

The factor pairs of $-45$ are

$$
(1,-45),\,\,(-1,45),\,\,(3,-15),\,\,(-3,15),\,\,(5,-9),\,\,(-5,9).
$$

Notice the numbers in the factor pair $(3,-15)$ add to $-12:$ 

$$
3-15=-12\,✓
$$

Then, rewrite the linear term as $3h-15h,$ and factor the result by grouping:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{h}^{2}-12h-9 & = \\ 5{h}^{2}+3h-15h-9 & = \\ 5{h}^{2}-15h+3h-9 & = \\ (5{h}^{2}-15h)+(3h-9) & = \\ 5h(h-3)+3(h-3) & = \\ (5h+3)(h-3) & \end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Factor 5h2−12h−9.

a
(5h−3)(h+3)
b
(5h+1)(h−3)
c
(5h+3)(h−3)
d
(5h+1)(h−9)
e
(5h+3)(h−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We must factor the quadratic expression 5h2−12h−9.

First, we find two numbers that

  • multiply to the product of the quadratic coefficient and the constant (5×−9=−45), and

  • add to the linear coefficient (−12).

The factor pairs of −45 are

(1,−45),(−1,45),(3,−15),(−3,15),(5,−9),(−5,9).

Notice the numbers in the factor pair (3,−15) add to −12:

3−15=−12✓

Then, rewrite the linear term as 3h−15h, and factor the result by grouping:

5h2−12h−9=5h2+3h−15h−9=5h2−15h+3h−9=(5h2−15h)+(3h−9)=5h(h−3)+3(h−3)=(5h+3)(h−3)
question.knowledge_point: Factoring Trinomials With Negative Constants

solution.reasoning: Expanding (5h+3)(h-3) gives 5h^2-15h+3h-9=5h^2-12h-9, so option c is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different quadratic.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & 23 \\ 23 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}c \\ 23\end{aligned}]
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 27 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 3 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 \\ -4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}17 & 23 \\ 23 & 85\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}13 \\ 23\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=17+85+13=115.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
questions.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{68}[\begin{aligned}68 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 18 \\ -8 & -16 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -16 \\ 36\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}25 & 50 \\ 50 & 100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}50 \\ 100\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 50 & 100 & 100\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=2-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2+\frac{(-2)}{1}=0.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $17a+\frac{b}{c}?$
questions.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {1}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & -6 \\ 2 & -4 \\ 4 & -8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & 1 \\ -6 & -4 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}17 & -34 \\ -34 & 68\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}17 & -34 & 3 \\ -34 & 68 & -6\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}17 & -34 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{3}{17}+2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{17}+2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}\frac{3}{17} \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
17a+\frac{b}{c}=17(\frac{3}{17})+\frac{2}{1}=5.
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}a & -8 \\ -8 & b\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ c\end{aligned}]
$$

what is the value of $a+b+c?$
questions.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {4}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 16\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 8 & 4 \\ -16 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}32 & -8 \\ -8 & 24\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=32+24+8=64.
$$

Question 1

A=[13−11−10],b=[1−10],W=[300020002]

Consider the matrices A and W, and the vector b above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem WAx=Wb is given by

[a2323b][x1x2]=[c23]

what is the value of a+b+c?

a
155
b
125
c
30
d
83
e
115
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To get the normal equation corresponding to WAx=Wb, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by (WA)T:

(WA)T⋅WAx=(WA)T⋅WbAT(WTW)Ax=AT(WTW)b

Now, since

WTW=[320002200022]=[900040004],

our normal equation can be written as follows:

[1−1−1310][900040004][13−11−10][x1x2]=[1−1−1310][900040004][1−10][1−1−1310][927−44−40][x1x2]=[1−1−1310][9−40][17232385][x1x2]=[1323]

Therefore, we have

a+b+c=17+85+13=115.

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{68}[\begin{aligned}68 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem WAx=Wb, where

A=[12−11−10],b=[3−42],W=[100020002].

a
[−22]
b
[22]
c
[23]
d
[1−1]
e
[−32]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To get the normal equation corresponding to WAx=Wb, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by (WA)T:

(WA)T⋅WAx=(WA)T⋅WbAT(WTW)Ax=AT(WTW)b

Now, since

WTW=[120002200022]=[100040004],

our normal equation can be written as follows:

[1−1−1210][100040004][12−11−10][x1x2]=[1−1−1210][100040004][3−42][1−1−1210][12−44−40][x1x2]=[1−1−1210][3−168][9−2−28][x1x2]=[11−10]

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

[x1x2]=[9−2−28]−1[11−10]=19⋅8−(−2)⋅(−2)[8229][11−10]=168[68−68]=[1−1].

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 18 \\ -8 & -16 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -16 \\ 36\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}25 & 50 \\ 50 & 100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}50 \\ 100\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 50 & 100 & 100\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=2-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2+\frac{(-2)}{1}=0.
$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
17a+\frac{b}{c}=17(\frac{3}{17})+\frac{2}{1}=5.
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
question.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{68}[\begin{aligned}68 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem WAx=Wb, where

A=[12−11−10],b=[3−42],W=[100020002].

a
[−22]
b
[22]
c
[23]
d
[1−1]
e
[−32]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To get the normal equation corresponding to WAx=Wb, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by (WA)T:

(WA)T⋅WAx=(WA)T⋅WbAT(WTW)Ax=AT(WTW)b

Now, since

WTW=[120002200022]=[100040004],

our normal equation can be written as follows:

[1−1−1210][100040004][12−11−10][x1x2]=[1−1−1210][100040004][3−42][1−1−1210][12−44−40][x1x2]=[1−1−1210][3−168][9−2−28][x1x2]=[11−10]

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

[x1x2]=[9−2−28]−1[11−10]=19⋅8−(−2)⋅(−2)[8229][11−10]=168[68−68]=[1−1].

last_observation.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{68}[\begin{aligned}68 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem WAx=Wb, where

A=[12−11−10],b=[3−42],W=[100020002].

a
[−22]
b
[22]
c
[23]
d
[1−1]
e
[−32]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To get the normal equation corresponding to WAx=Wb, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by (WA)T:

(WA)T⋅WAx=(WA)T⋅WbAT(WTW)Ax=AT(WTW)b

Now, since

WTW=[120002200022]=[100040004],

our normal equation can be written as follows:

[1−1−1210][100040004][12−11−10][x1x2]=[1−1−1210][100040004][3−42][1−1−1210][12−44−40][x1x2]=[1−1−1210][3−168][9−2−28][x1x2]=[11−10]

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

[x1x2]=[9−2−28]−1[11−10]=19⋅8−(−2)⋅(−2)[8229][11−10]=168[68−68]=[1−1].

solution.reasoning: The normal equation is A^T W^T W A x=A^T W^T W b. Here W^T W=diag(1,4,4), giving 9x_1-2x_2=11 and -2x_1+8x_2=-10. Solving yields x_1=1 and x_2=-1. The coefficient matrix has determinant 68, so this is the unique least-squares solution, current option d. No Math Academy answer or grade is captured to verify its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
Find the solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb,$ where

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{1}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {2}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -4 & 4 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 \\ -16 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the matrix on the left-hand side is invertible, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & ={[\begin{aligned}9 & -2 \\ -2 & 8\end{aligned}]}^{-1}[\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{9\cdot 8-(-2)\cdot (-2)}[\begin{aligned}8 & 2 \\ 2 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}11 \\ -10\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{68}[\begin{aligned}68 \\ -68\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
