question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Consider the matrices $A$ and $W,$ and the vector $b$ shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem $W\,Ax=Wb$ is 

$$
[\begin{aligned}a \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}b \\ c\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R,
$$

what is the value of  $a+\frac{b}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 18 \\ -8 & -16 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -16 \\ 36\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}25 & 50 \\ 50 & 100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}50 \\ 100\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 50 & 100 & 100\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=2-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2+\frac{(-2)}{1}=0.
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

A=[12−2−400],b=[2−44],W=[300020003].

Consider the matrices A and W, and the vector b shown above. If the general solution for the weighted least-squares problem WAx=Wb is [a0]+x2[bc],x2∈R, what is the value of a+bc?

a
7
b
0
c
10
d
9
e
12
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To get the normal equation corresponding to WAx=Wb, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by (WA)T:

(WA)T⋅WAx=(WA)T⋅WbAT(WTW)Ax=AT(WTW)b

Now, since

WTW=[320002200032]=[900040009],

our normal equation can be written as follows:

[1−202−40][900040009][12−2−400][x1x2]=[1−202−40][900040009][2−44][1−202−40][918−8−1600][x1x2]=[1−202−40][18−1636][255050100][x1x2]=[50100]

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows: M=[25505050100100]R2:=R2−2R1∼[255050000]

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the 1st one). Thus, x2 is a free variable. From the first equation, we have x1=2−2x2.

Hence, the general solution is

[2−2x2x2]=[20]+x2[−21],x2∈R.

Therefore, we have

a+bc=2+(−2)1=0.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}(W\,A)^{T}\cdot W\,Ax & =(W\,A)^{T}\cdot Wb \\ {A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)Ax & ={A}^{T}({W}^{T}W)b\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since

$$
{W}^{T}W=[\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & {3}^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}],
$$

our normal equation can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 9\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ -4 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}9 & 18 \\ -8 & -16 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -4 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}18 \\ -16 \\ 36\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}25 & 50 \\ 50 & 100\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}50 \\ 100\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve the system corresponding to the above matrix equation using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 50 & 100 & 100\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}25 & 50 & 50 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we have 

$$
{x}_{1}=2-2{x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}2-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+\frac{b}{c}=2+\frac{(-2)}{1}=0.
$$

solution.reasoning: Let s=x_1+2x_2. The squared weighted residual is 9(s-2)^2+4(-2s+4)^2+9(0-4)^2=25(s-2)^2+144, minimized when s=2. Thus the general solution is [2,0]^T+x_2[-2,1]^T, giving a=2, b=-2, c=1 and a+b/c=0, current option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade verifies its key.

question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,b=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,W=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4\end{aligned}]

question.worked_solution:
To get the normal equation corresponding to $W\,Ax=Wb,$ we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by $(W\,A)^{T}:$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
a+b+c=32+24+8=64.
$$

\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 8 & 4 \\ -16 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}32 & -8 \\ -8 & 24\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
a+b+c=32+24+8=64.
$$

Question 5
?

A=[0221−11],b=[210],W=[100020004]

Consider the matrices A and W, and the vector b above. If the normal equation for the corresponding weighted least-squares problem WAx=Wb is given by

[a−8−8b][x1x2]=[8c]

what is the value of a+b+c?

a
72
b
56
c
48
d
64
e
40
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To get the normal equation corresponding to WAx=Wb, we pre-multiply both sides of the equation by (WA)T:

(WA)T⋅WAx=(WA)T⋅WbAT(WTW)Ax=AT(WTW)b

Now, since

WTW=[120002200042]=[1000400016],

our normal equation can be written as follows:

[02−1211][1000400016][0221−11][x1x2]=[02−1211][1000400016][210][02−1211][0284−1616][x1x2]=[02−1211][240][32−8−824][x1x2]=[88]

Therefore, we have

a+b+c=32+24+8=64.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1-t+2{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 8 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+t+{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=1+t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =(-1)\cdot (1+t+{t}^{2})+1\cdot (1+t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-1-t-{t}^{2}+1+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =-2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+2t+3{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=-3-t-2{t}^{3}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =3\cdot (1+2t+3{t}^{2})+(-1)\cdot (-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =3+6t+9{t}^{2}-(-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =6+7t+9{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & -4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-1 \\ -4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-8 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -12 \\ 0 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-1 \\ 6{x}_{2}=-12 \\ -4{x}_{2}=8.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2\cdot (-2) & =-1 \\ {x}_{1} & =-1+4 \\ {x}_{1} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-2)=1.$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}9 & -18 \\ 15 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -18 \\ 15 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -18 \\ 15 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=9 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-18 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=15.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 9 \\ -2 & 2 & -18 \\ 3 & 1 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 9 \\ -2 & 2 & -18 \\ 3 & 1 & 15\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=9 \\ 3{x}_{2}=-9 \\ -\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =9 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-3) & =9 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=6+(-3)=3.$

{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 20 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 20 & -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 20 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=4 \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=20 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 20 \\ -2 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 20 \\ -2 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 7 & 14 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=4 \\ 7{x}_{2}=14 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2\cdot 2 & =4 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =8 \\ {x}_{1} & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=4+2=6.$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & 3{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} & {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ -{x}_{1}=-2 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{4}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ {x}_{2}=3 \\ -4{x}_{2}=-12.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second,  third and fourth equations, we get ${x}_{2}=3.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3 & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Finally, $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2\cdot 2+3=7.$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ 0 & \frac{9}{2} & \frac{9}{2} \\ 0 & -\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=-2 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2}=\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{5}{2}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=1.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6\cdot 1 & =-2 \\ 4{x}_{1} & =-8 \\ {x}_{1} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2+1=-1.$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Consider the following polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2+t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=1-{t}^{2},\,q(t)=2+3t+4{t}^{2}.
$$

If $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\},$ and $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
questions.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2+t)+{x}_{2}(1-{t}^{2}) & =2+3t+4{t}^{2} \\ (2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{1}t-{x}_{2}{t}^{2} & =2+3t+4{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ {x}_{1}=3 \\ -{x}_{2}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-4.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+(-4)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-4)=-1.$

\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({t}^{2}+t)+{x}_{2}({t}^{2}-2t+4)+{x}_{3}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-2) & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3} \\ (4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})t+({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}){t}^{2}+{x}_{3}{t}^{3} & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=1 \\ {x}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=1.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
4{x}_{2}-2\cdot 1=2\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained value into the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}-2\cdot 1=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{1}=2.$

$$

$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=4 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].

$$
{x}_{1}+(2)=4\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.

questions.worked_solution:

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t)=q(t).
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-6{t}^{3}+6t+12)+{x}_{2}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-3t-2)+{x}_{3}(-3{t}^{2}+2t) & =-9{t}^{3}+19t+18 \\ (-6{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){t}^{3}+(-2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}){t}^{2}+(6{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3})t+(12{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}) & =-9{t}^{3}+19t+18.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-9 \\ -2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=19 \\ 12{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=18.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 6 & -3 & 2 & 19 \\ 12 & -2 & 0 & 18\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 6 & -3 & 2 & 19 \\ 12 & -2 & 0 & 18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-9 \\ -2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
-2{x}_{2}-3\cdot 2=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained values into the first equation, we get

$$
-6{x}_{1}+(-3)=-9\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{2}=-3.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-2 \\ {x}_{3}=-2 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-1){R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=-2 \\ {x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the  third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
2{x}_{2}+3(-2)=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=2.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained values into the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}+(2)+2(-2)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{1}=2.$

Example: 
                    Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the polynomials $p_1(t)$ and $p_2(t),$ given by

$$
p_1(t)=3+2t, \qquad
	p_2(t)=-t+t^2.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/9eca81c24ee88a63d1c5468160a118cb1e987793d5fdc8d2d7eaa317fadeda93.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/8c3fce8e9d7cc170ad66706e783c4a46ba0530c119b8b824a66d9b5850e62760.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =4\cdot (3+2t)+(-3)\cdot (-t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =12+8t+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =12+11t-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

If $\mathcal B = \{B_1,B_2\}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{ B_1, B_2 \},$ calculate ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/9b978860f45e9e62e0315727c8eafac13360f29a7762480103b087ed6babf376.svg)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 B_1 +x_2 B_2 = A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 8 & -4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} & 0 \\ 8{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & -4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-5 \\ 8{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/88ea80808ca87358b78cf322c8ddd81ad7f95ddc02526361aace1ca9b914d486.svg)

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & -5 \\ 8 & -2 & -2 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 18 \\ 0 & -1 & -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-5 \\ 2{x}_{2}=18 \\ -{x}_{2}=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get $x_2 =9.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-9 & =-5 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =4 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Matrix Vector Space

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following polynomials:

$$
p_1(t)=5+t^2, \quad
p_2(t)=3t-2t^2, \quad
q(t)=5-3t+3t^2.
$$

If $\mathcal{B}=\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\},$ find $[q(t)]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We need to find $x_1$ and $x_2$ such that 

$$
x_1 p_1(t)+x_2 p_2(t) = q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(5+{t}^{2})+{x}_{2}(3t-2{t}^{2}) & =5-3t+3{t}^{2} \\ 5{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}t+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =5-3t+3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=-3 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/271f2b051a53f7aeae9a20ef23b97c9c903a7815f228dfa3ee23e2207bd24ee9.svg)

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 1 & -2 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-\frac{1}{5}){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & -2 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+\frac{2}{3}{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}5 & 0 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & -3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}5{x}_{1}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=-3.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first and second equations, we get $x_1=1$ and $x_2 =-1.$ Therefore, ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/1fc60fff97ff92bd1cc515e6c984fbacb435dcf0fae24e751842eb8daf3390e8.svg)

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/2828c037a750f078b4d98b93248e800ec05d4899d7eb390dd135326314c44e70.svg)

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/2db3ab1e4452eff2f19151cc87a805452433c7f305a80e5480c25241cba42c38.svg)

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/6489e130a9237881664e1649cc5408cdff87cfb12dcf44c0342b9961cdf7bc81.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/2828c037a750f078b4d98b93248e800ec05d4899d7eb390dd135326314c44e70.svg)

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/2db3ab1e4452eff2f19151cc87a805452433c7f305a80e5480c25241cba42c38.svg)

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/6489e130a9237881664e1649cc5408cdff87cfb12dcf44c0342b9961cdf7bc81.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.problem:
Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/c9297a30f87baf08295a752cb23f2d314139508f875b4ffa2fffc8763656bd54.svg)

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq 1.$

tutorial.content:
We've already seen how to write the coordinates of a vector $\mathbf v\in \mathbb R^n$ relative some general basis $\mathcal B$ of $\mathbb R^n.$ In this lesson, we will generalize this concept to abstract vector spaces.

As an example, consider the matrices $A_1$ and $A_2,$ given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/300c1d872cdd3217c0499e0bbb7294b7bb2fd26774dca8afa69bd14069cdc3a5.svg)

The set $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ is a basis of the vector space $V = \textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}.$ Now, suppose that the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/80e5d9a9286b363d1b9b766cea9991c6329af1703dd00959f01c57919d3fb889.svg)

Let's find the matrix $C$ using this information. 

As usual, any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ A_1, A_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
x_1 A_1  + x_2 A_2,
$$

where $x_1,x_2$ are the coordinates of the vector relative to the basis. 

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/e8feab375d52d5f50b40369b73f6705b0fd9f47718668846e10c5a9bbab3c23c.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =2\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}]+4\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 3 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ 0 & 10\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}0 & 12 \\ 8 & -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 10 \\ 8 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
tutorial.title: Introduction

observed_steps.name: Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/41a4f8d266d67bbe48e91aefa7b4a09f53143b3218ea68b1df9d2ee9e1f373d5.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =4\cdot (3+2t)+(-3)\cdot (-t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =12+8t+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =12+11t-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials $p_1(t)$ and $p_2(t),$ given by

$$
p_1(t)=3+2t, \qquad
	p_2(t)=-t+t^2.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $\mathcal{B}=\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t) \big\}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ are ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/12219bddf4479a5d4578e022bae46d09b38b2499486f3ee59eafb30c2ed1f074.svg)
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\textrm{Span}\big\{ p_1, p_2 \big\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/41a4f8d266d67bbe48e91aefa7b4a09f53143b3218ea68b1df9d2ee9e1f373d5.svg)

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =4\cdot (3+2t)+(-3)\cdot (-t+{t}^{2}) \\  & =12+8t+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =12+11t-3{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1-t+2{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1−t+2t2,p2(t)=t−t2. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[13].

a
p(t)=1+4t−t2
b
p(t)=1+2t−5t2
c
p(t)=1+2t−6t2
d
p(t)=1+2t−t2
e
p(t)=1−3t−t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[13].

Therefore,

p(t)=1⋅(1−t+2t2)+3⋅(t−t2)=1−t+2t2+3t−3t2=1+2t−t2.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =(-1)\cdot (1+t+{t}^{2})+1\cdot (1+t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-1-t-{t}^{2}+1+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =-2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1+2t+3t2,p2(t)=−3−t−2t3. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[3−1].

a
p(t)=6+7t+9t2+2t3
b
p(t)=−6t+9t2+2t3
c
p(t)=5t+9t2+2t3
d
p(t)=7t+9t2+2t3
e
p(t)=6+5t+9t2+2t3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[3−1].

Therefore,

p(t)=3⋅(1+2t+3t2)+(−1)⋅(−3−t−2t3)=3+6t+9t2−(−3−t−2t3)=6+7t+9t2+2t3.

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 8 & -4\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2} & 0 \\ 8{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & -4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-5 \\ 8{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -4{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/09c741f685a5e1fdf9af602d7e117af4c50d838ea09f15871f370668355da8b6.svg)

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & -5 \\ 8 & -2 & -2 \\ -4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & -5 \\ 0 & 2 & 18 \\ 0 & -1 & -9\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=-5 \\ 2{x}_{2}=18 \\ -{x}_{2}=-9.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get $x_2 =9.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-9 & =-5 \\ 2{x}_{1} & =4 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Question 6
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Matrix Vector Space
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & -4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-1 \\ -4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-8 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -12 \\ 0 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-1 \\ 6{x}_{2}=-12 \\ -4{x}_{2}=8.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2\cdot (-2) & =-1 \\ {x}_{1} & =-1+4 \\ {x}_{1} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-2)=1.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ -{x}_{1}=-2 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$

$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2+t)+{x}_{2}(1-{t}^{2}) & =2+3t+4{t}^{2} \\ (2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{1}t-{x}_{2}{t}^{2} & =2+3t+4{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ {x}_{1}=3 \\ -{x}_{2}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-4.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+(-4)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-4)=-1.$

observed_steps.name: Question 12
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Coordinates of a Vector With Respect to a Given Basis in a Polynomial Vector Space
observed_steps.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t)=q(t).
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({t}^{2}+t)+{x}_{2}({t}^{2}-2t+4)+{x}_{3}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-2) & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3} \\ (4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})t+({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}){t}^{2}+{x}_{3}{t}^{3} & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=1 \\ {x}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=1.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
4{x}_{2}-2\cdot 1=2\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained value into the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}-2\cdot 1=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{1}=2.$

tutorial.name: Isomorphisms of Vector Spaces
tutorial.problem:
Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/ad006b7ef64d5e272705fe838722e754d432fc483e948af1701b75026053f4d8.svg)

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq 1.$

tutorial.content:
Suppose we fix a basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1, \mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ of a finite-dimensional vector space $V$ with scalars from $\mathbb{R}$ (note that "finite-dimensional" means that the basis contains a finite number of elements). Then, we can represent any element $\mathbf{v} \in V$ using the coordinates of $\mathbf{v}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14159472/assets/ad006b7ef64d5e272705fe838722e754d432fc483e948af1701b75026053f4d8.svg)

This defines a bijective mapping $\phi: V\to \mathbb{R}^n.$ Moreover, this particular mapping has some nice properties:

- $\phi(\mathbf{u}+\mathbf{v}) = \phi(\mathbf{u}) + \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{v} \in V,$ and

- $\phi(\alpha \mathbf{v}) = \alpha \phi(\mathbf{v})$ for any $\mathbf{v} \in V$ and any $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}.$

Because of this, we say that $V$ is **isomorphic** to $\mathbb{R}^n.$ Intuitively, this means that $V$ and $\mathbb R^n$ have identical structures.

So, any finite-dimensional vector space is isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}^n$ for some particular $n.$ This means that instead of studying all possible vector spaces, we can simply study only one family of vector spaces, namely $\mathbb{R}^n$ for $n\geq 1.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1-t+2{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1−t+2t2,p2(t)=t−t2. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[13].

a
p(t)=1+4t−t2
b
p(t)=1+2t−5t2
c
p(t)=1+2t−6t2
d
p(t)=1+2t−t2
e
p(t)=1−3t−t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[13].

Therefore,

p(t)=1⋅(1−t+2t2)+3⋅(t−t2)=1−t+2t2+3t−3t2=1+2t−t2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1-t+2{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:

$$

$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1−t+2t2,p2(t)=t−t2. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[13].

a
p(t)=1+4t−t2
b
p(t)=1+2t−5t2
c
p(t)=1+2t−6t2
d
p(t)=1+2t−t2
e
p(t)=1−3t−t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[13].

Therefore,

p(t)=1⋅(1−t+2t2)+3⋅(t−t2)=1−t+2t2+3t−3t2=1+2t−t2.

feedback.name: Question 1
feedback.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1-t+2{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =1\cdot (1-t+2{t}^{2})+3\cdot (t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =1-t+2{t}^{2}+3t-3{t}^{2} \\  & =1+2t-{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1−t+2t2,p2(t)=t−t2. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[13].

a
p(t)=1+4t−t2
b
p(t)=1+2t−5t2
c
p(t)=1+2t−6t2
d
p(t)=1+2t−t2
e
p(t)=1−3t−t2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[13].

Therefore,

p(t)=1⋅(1−t+2t2)+3⋅(t−t2)=1−t+2t2+3t−3t2=1+2t−t2.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

A1=[01−12],A2=[1120]

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix C given that B={A1,A2} is a basis of Span{A1,A2}, and the coordinates of the matrix C relative to B are [C]B=[−22].

a
[026−4]
b
[20−46]
c
[2−460]
d
[206−4]
e
[602−4]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{A1,A2} can be written as

x1A1+x2A2.

In our case, we have

[C]B=[x1x2]=[−22].

Therefore, C=(−2)⋅[01−12]+2⋅[1120]=[0−22−4]+[2240]=[206−4].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

A1=[01−12],A2=[1120]

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix C given that B={A1,A2} is a basis of Span{A1,A2}, and the coordinates of the matrix C relative to B are [C]B=[−22].

a
[026−4]
b
[20−46]
c
[2−460]
d
[206−4]
e
[602−4]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{A1,A2} can be written as

x1A1+x2A2.

In our case, we have

[C]B=[x1x2]=[−22].

Therefore, C=(−2)⋅[01−12]+2⋅[1120]=[0−22−4]+[2240]=[206−4].
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis

solution.reasoning: The basis coordinates mean C=-2A_1+2A_2. Entrywise addition gives C=[[2,0],[6,-4]], matching option d. No captured answer or grade establishes Math Academy's key for this question; the supplied worked solution concerns a different example.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =(-2)\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]+2\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 2 & -4\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 8 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
last_observation.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 8 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Question 3
?

A1=[−112−3],A2=[1102]

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix C given that B={A1,A2} is a basis of Span{A1,A2}, and the coordinates of the matrix C relative to B are [C]B=[43].

a
[−194−6]
b
[−1−723]
c
[−178−6]
d
[1586]
e
[−254−3]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{A1,A2} can be written as

x1A1+x2A2.

In our case, we have

[C]B=[x1x2]=[43].

Therefore, C=4⋅[−112−3]+3⋅[1102]=[−448−12]+[3306]=[−178−6].
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis

solution.reasoning: The coordinates give C=4A_1+3A_2. Its entries are -4+3=-1, 4+3=7, 8+0=8, and -12+6=-6, matching option c. The supplied example explains the method but provides no Math Academy answer evidence for this question.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
$$
{A}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}],\,{A}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Find the matrix $C$ given that $B=\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of the matrix $C$ relative to $B$ are $[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Any vector in $\text{Span}\{{A}_{1},{A}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{A}_{1}+{x}_{2}{A}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[C]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}C & =4\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 2 & -3\end{aligned}]+3\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 4 \\ 8 & -12\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}3 & 3 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 7 \\ 8 & -6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+t+{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=1+t-{t}^{2}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =(-1)\cdot (1+t+{t}^{2})+1\cdot (1+t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-1-t-{t}^{2}+1+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =-2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =(-1)\cdot (1+t+{t}^{2})+1\cdot (1+t-{t}^{2}) \\  & =-1-t-{t}^{2}+1+t-{t}^{2} \\  & =-2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+2t+3{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=-3-t-2{t}^{3}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$
question.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =3\cdot (1+2t+3{t}^{2})+(-1)\cdot (-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =3+6t+9{t}^{2}-(-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =6+7t+9{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1+2t+3t2,p2(t)=−3−t−2t3. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[3−1].

a
p(t)=6+7t+9t2+2t3
b
p(t)=−6t+9t2+2t3
c
p(t)=5t+9t2+2t3
d
p(t)=7t+9t2+2t3
e
p(t)=6+5t+9t2+2t3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[3−1].

Therefore,

p(t)=3⋅(1+2t+3t2)+(−1)⋅(−3−t−2t3)=3+6t+9t2−(−3−t−2t3)=6+7t+9t2+2t3.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis
last_observation.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =3\cdot (1+2t+3{t}^{2})+(-1)\cdot (-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =3+6t+9{t}^{2}-(-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =6+7t+9{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+2t+3{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=-3-t-2{t}^{3}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Consider the polynomials p1(t) and p2(t), given by p1(t)=1+2t+3t2,p2(t)=−3−t−2t3. Find p(t) given that B={p1(t),p2(t)} is a basis of Span{p1,p2}, and the coordinates of p(t) relative to B are [p(t)]B=[3−1].

a
p(t)=6+7t+9t2+2t3
b
p(t)=−6t+9t2+2t3
c
p(t)=5t+9t2+2t3
d
p(t)=7t+9t2+2t3
e
p(t)=6+5t+9t2+2t3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Any vector in Span{p1,p2} can be written as

x1p1(t)+x2p2(t).

In our case, we have

[p(t)]B=[x1x2]=[3−1].

Therefore,

p(t)=3⋅(1+2t+3t2)+(−1)⋅(−3−t−2t3)=3+6t+9t2−(−3−t−2t3)=6+7t+9t2+2t3.
question.knowledge_point: Calculating a Vector Given Its Coordinates Relative to a Basis

solution.reasoning: The coordinates give p(t)=3p_1(t)-p_2(t)=3+6t+9t^2+3+t+2t^3=6+7t+9t^2+2t^3, matching option a. The supplied worked example supports the method but does not establish Math Academy's answer key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
Consider the polynomials ${p}_{1}(t)$ and ${p}_{2}(t),$ given by

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+2t+3{t}^{2},\,{p}_{2}(t)=-3-t-2{t}^{3}.
$$

Find $p(t)$ given that $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\},$ and the coordinates of $p(t)$ relative to $B$ are $[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].$
feedback.worked_solution:
Any vector in  $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1},{p}_{2}\}$ can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t).\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
[p(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}p(t) & =3\cdot (1+2t+3{t}^{2})+(-1)\cdot (-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =3+6t+9{t}^{2}-(-3-t-2{t}^{3}) \\  & =6+7t+9{t}^{2}+2{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -4 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & -4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -8 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-1 \\ -4{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-8 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=7.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ -4 & -2 & -8 \\ 1 & -2 & 7\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 0 & 6 & -12 \\ 0 & -4 & 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-1 \\ 6{x}_{2}=-12 \\ -4{x}_{2}=8.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-2.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+2\cdot (-2) & =-1 \\ {x}_{1} & =-1+4 \\ {x}_{1} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-2)=1.$

feedback.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}9 & -18 \\ 15 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -18 \\ 15 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}9 & -18 \\ 15 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=9 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-18 \\ 3{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=15.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 9 \\ -2 & 2 & -18 \\ 3 & 1 & 15\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 9 \\ -2 & 2 & -18 \\ 3 & 1 & 15\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 9 \\ 0 & 3 & -9 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & \frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=9 \\ 3{x}_{2}=-9 \\ -\frac{{x}_{2}}{2}=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=-3.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} & =9 \\ 2{x}_{1}+(-3) & =9 \\ {x}_{1} & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}6 \\ -3\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=6+(-3)=3.$

question.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 20 & -2\end{aligned}]

question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 3 & -2\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}0 & -2 \\ 4 & 3\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 20 & -2\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}0 & 2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2} & -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 20 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=4 \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=20 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 20 \\ -2 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4 & 20 \\ -2 & 3 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & 7 & 14 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=4 \\ 3{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=20 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=-2.\end{aligned}

$$
