question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & 3{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} & {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ -{x}_{1}=-2 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{4}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ {x}_{2}=3 \\ -4{x}_{2}=-12.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second,  third and fourth equations, we get ${x}_{2}=3.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3 & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Finally, $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2\cdot 2+3=7.$

a
4
b
5

EXPLANATION

We need to find x1 and x2 such that

x1B1+x2B2=A.

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

{2x1−2x2=−23x2=9−x1=−2x1+x2=5.

feedback.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
feedback.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} & 3{x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} & {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 9 \\ -2 & 5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=-2 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ -{x}_{1}=-2 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -2 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 5\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{4}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ -1 & 0 & -2 \\ 2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-2){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 3 & 9 \\ 0 & 1 & 3 \\ 0 & -4 & -12\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=5 \\ 3{x}_{2}=9 \\ {x}_{2}=3 \\ -4{x}_{2}=-12.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second,  third and fourth equations, we get ${x}_{2}=3.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3 & =5 \\ {x}_{1} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

Finally, $2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2\cdot 2+3=7.$

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Consider the following matrices:

$$
{B}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{B}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

If $B=\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{B}_{1},{B}_{2}\},$ and $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{B}_{1}+{x}_{2}{B}_{2}=A.
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}[\begin{aligned}4 & -1 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}]+{x}_{2}[\begin{aligned}6 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & 0\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 5 \\ -4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=-2 \\ -{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}=5 \\ 3{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ -1 & 3 & 5 \\ 3 & 2 & -4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{4}{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}4 & 6 & -2 \\ 0 & \frac{9}{2} & \frac{9}{2} \\ 0 & -\frac{5}{2} & -\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6{x}_{2}=-2 \\ \frac{9}{2}{x}_{2}=\frac{9}{2} \\ -\frac{5}{2}{x}_{2}=-\frac{5}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third equations, we get ${x}_{2}=1.$ From the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1}+6\cdot 1 & =-2 \\ 4{x}_{1} & =-8 \\ {x}_{1} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, $[A]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-2+1=-1.$

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
Consider the following polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=2+t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=1-{t}^{2},\,q(t)=2+3t+4{t}^{2}.
$$

If $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\},$ and $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2+t)+{x}_{2}(1-{t}^{2}) & =2+3t+4{t}^{2} \\ (2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+{x}_{1}t-{x}_{2}{t}^{2} & =2+3t+4{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ {x}_{1}=3 \\ -{x}_{2}=4.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{1}{2}){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second equation, we get ${x}_{2}=-4.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
2{x}_{1}+(-4)=2\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=3.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -4\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=3+(-4)=-1.$

question.name: Question 12
question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t)=q(t).
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({t}^{2}+t)+{x}_{2}({t}^{2}-2t+4)+{x}_{3}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-2) & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3} \\ (4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})t+({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}){t}^{2}+{x}_{3}{t}^{3} & =2+{t}^{2}+{t}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=1 \\ {x}_{3}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{2} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 & -2 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=0 \\ 4{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=2 \\ -\frac{1}{2}{x}_{3}=-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=1.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
4{x}_{2}-2\cdot 1=2\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=1.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained value into the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}-2\cdot 1=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{1}=2.$

Consider the following polynomials:

$$
{p}_{1}(t)=1+t,\,{p}_{2}(t)=1-t+{t}^{2},\,q(t)=4+2{t}^{2}.
$$

If $B=\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\}$ is a basis of $\text{Span}\{{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)\},$ and $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],$ then ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=$
question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=q(t)
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(1+t)+{x}_{2}(1-t+{t}^{2}) & =4+2{t}^{2} \\ ({x}_{1}+{x}_{2})+({x}_{1}-{x}_{2})t+{x}_{2}{t}^{2} & =4+2{t}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=4 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

 

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=4 \\ -2{x}_{2}=-4 \\ {x}_{2}=2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the second and third  equations, we get ${x}_{2}=2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

$$
{x}_{1}+(2)=4\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$

Finally, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=2+2=4.$

question.worked_solution:
We need to find ${x}_{1},{x}_{2}$ and ${x}_{3}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t)=q(t).
$$

Substituting the given information into the above equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(-6{t}^{3}+6t+12)+{x}_{2}({t}^{3}-2{t}^{2}-3t-2)+{x}_{3}(-3{t}^{2}+2t) & =-9{t}^{3}+19t+18 \\ (-6{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){t}^{3}+(-2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}){t}^{2}+(6{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3})t+(12{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}) & =-9{t}^{3}+19t+18.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the coefficients of $t$, we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-9 \\ -2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 6{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=19 \\ 12{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}=18.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 6 & -3 & 2 & 19 \\ 12 & -2 & 0 & 18\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 6 & -3 & 2 & 19 \\ 12 & -2 & 0 & 18\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 2 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}-6 & 1 & 0 & -9 \\ 0 & -2 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 5 & 10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=-9 \\ -2{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ 5{x}_{3}=10.\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
-2{x}_{2}-3\cdot 2=0\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=-3.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained values into the first equation, we get

$$
-6{x}_{1}+(-3)=-9\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=1.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3 \\ 2\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{2}=-3.$

\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-2 \\ {x}_{3}=-2 \\ {x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

 

The equations above give a linear system with the augmented matrix

$$
M=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Row-reducing the matrix using Gaussian elimination, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M= & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & -1 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-1){R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\ ∼ & [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now 

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=-2 \\ {x}_{3}=-2.\end{aligned}
$$

From the  third equation, we get ${x}_{3}=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we get

$$
2{x}_{2}+3(-2)=-2\,⟹\,{x}_{2}=2.
$$

Now, substituting the obtained values into the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}+(2)+2(-2)=0\,⟹\,{x}_{1}=2.
$$

Therefore, $[q(t)]_{B}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],$ and therefore ${x}_{1}=2.$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the value of $(-\frac{3}{8})÷\frac{1}{6}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Dividing a negative number by a positive number gives a negative number. Hence, the result will be negative.

Therefore, since 

$$
\frac{3}{8}÷\frac{1}{6}=\frac{3\times 6}{8\times 1}=\frac{18}{8}=\frac{9}{4},
$$

we obtain

$$
(-\frac{3}{8})÷\frac{1}{6}=-\frac{9}{4}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Determine the value of $(-\frac{1}{5})÷(-\frac{3}{10}).$
questions.worked_solution:
Dividing a negative number by a negative number gives a positive number. Hence, the result will be positive.

Therefore, since 

$$
\frac{1}{5}÷\frac{3}{10}=\frac{1\times 10}{5\times 3}=\frac{10}{15}=\frac{2}{3},
$$

we obtain

$$
(-\frac{1}{5})÷(-\frac{3}{10})=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

43
d

Correct
EXPLANATION

Dividing a negative number by a positive number gives a negative number. Hence, the result will be negative.

Therefore, since 38÷16=3×68×1=188=94, we obtain (−38)÷16=−94.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Determine the value of $(-\frac{1}{5})÷(-\frac{3}{10}).$
question.worked_solution:
Dividing a negative number by a negative number gives a positive number. Hence, the result will be positive.

Therefore, since 

$$
\frac{1}{5}÷\frac{3}{10}=\frac{1\times 10}{5\times 3}=\frac{10}{15}=\frac{2}{3},
$$

we obtain

$$
(-\frac{1}{5})÷(-\frac{3}{10})=\frac{2}{3}.
$$

we obtain

$$
(-6)÷\frac{12}{5}=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
A particle of mass $0.4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force $F(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
A particle of mass $0.5\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force 

$$
F(t)=(3{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2})\,\text{N}
$$

is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.5{y}^{″}=-ky+(3{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-\frac{3}{2}).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+2ky=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=2k\,⟹\,k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1)$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$ Since

$$
f(t)=3(2{cos}^{2}⁡(2t)-1)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),
$$

the frequency of the external periodic force is $4.$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{1}{2}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\cdot {4}^{2}=8\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[16(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 16D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{8}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

questions.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
questions.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[8(D-2Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8(C+2Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 8D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{3}{4}$ and $D=1.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

A particle of mass $0.4\,\text{kg}$ is attached to a massless spring. An external periodic force $F(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t)\,\text{N}$ is applied to the particle.

The position of the particle is $y(t)$ (measured in meters), and $t>0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle moves with forced harmonic motion without damping and the system experiences resonance, what is the spring constant $k?$

$k=$
{{field-1}}${\text{kg/s}}^{2}$
question.worked_solution:
The equation of motion for a particle of mass $m$ moving with forced harmonic motion without damping under the action of a spring with spring constant $k$ and external force $F(t)$ is given by

$$
m{y}^{″}=-ky+F(t).
$$

Substituting our values for $m$ and $F(t)$ gives

$$
0.4{y}^{″}=-ky+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

Simplifying and rearranging the above equation, we get

$$
{y}^{″}+\frac{5k}{2}y=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t).
$$

The complementary solution ${y}_{c}$ here represents simple harmonic motion, and it can be written as

$$
{y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t,
$$

where $A$ and $B$ are arbitrary constants of integration, and $\omega $ is the system's internal frequency.

In our case,

$$
{\omega }^{2}=\frac{5k}{2}\,⟹\,k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}.
$$

The oscillator experiences resonance when the frequency of the external periodic force $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(5t),$ which is $5,$ is equal to the frequency of the complementary solution $\omega .$

Therefore,

$$
k=\frac{2}{5}{\omega }^{2}=\frac{2}{5}\cdot {5}^{2}=10\,{\text{kg/s}}^{2}.
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)-\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
question.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[16(D-Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16(C+Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t) \\ 16D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-16C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =5\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=0$ and $D=\frac{5}{8}.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{5}{8}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Only solution II matches the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "II only".

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

solution.reasoning: At resonance, y''+16y=8\cos(4t)-6\sin(4t). The identities (d²/dt²+16)[t\cos(4t)]=-8\sin(4t) and (d²/dt²+16)[t\sin(4t)]=8\cos(4t) show that (3/4)t\cos(4t)+t\sin(4t) is a particular solution. Each displayed homogeneous term represents the full family A\cos(4t)+B\sin(4t), so I, II, and III are valid. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was provided.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem:
A particle is moving with forced harmonic motion without damping. The particle is acted on by an external periodic force
$f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).$
Assuming the system experiences resonance, which of the following could be used to represent the general solution for the position $y(t)?$

I. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

II. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

III. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Note that $A,$ $B,$ $R,$ and $ϕ$ are constants.
feedback.worked_solution:
Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency $\omega .$

The external force is $f(t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),$ which is sinusoidal with frequency $4.$ Therefore,
$\omega =4.$

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

1\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

2\. ${y}_{c}=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(\omega t+ϕ)=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)$

3\. ${y}_{c}=A\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t+B\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency $\omega $ duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by $t$ and take a resonant particular solution of the form

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)).
$$

By substituting the particular solution and $\omega =4$ into the differential equation, ${y}^{″}+{\omega }^{2}y=f(t),$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}[8(D-2Ct)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8(C+2Dt)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)]+16t(C\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+D\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) \\ 8D\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-8C\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t) & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)\end{aligned}
$$

Equating coefficients, $C=\frac{3}{4}$ and $D=1.$ 

So, the particular solution is

$$
{y}_{p}(t)=\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t).
$$

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

1\. $y=R\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

2\. $y=R\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t+ϕ)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

3\. $y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+\frac{3}{4}t\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)+t\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)$

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above.
Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".

a

None

Submit

Because the motion is undamped and the system experiences resonance, the forcing frequency equals the natural frequency ω.

The external force is f(t)=8cos⁡(4t)−6sin⁡(4t), which is sinusoidal with frequency 4. Therefore, ω=4.

The complementary solution for the associated simple harmonic motion equation can be written in three different forms:

  1. yc=Rcos⁡(ωt+ϕ)=Rcos⁡(4t+ϕ)

  2. yc=Rsin⁡(ωt+ϕ)=Rsin⁡(4t+ϕ)

  3. yc=Acos⁡ωt+Bsin⁡ωt=Acos⁡(4t)+Bsin⁡(4t)

At resonance, a sinusoidal trial at frequency ω duplicates the complementary solution, so we multiply by t and take a resonant particular solution of the form yp(t)=t(Ccos⁡(4t)+Dsin⁡(4t)).

Equating coefficients, C=34 and D=1.

So, the particular solution is yp(t)=34tcos⁡(4t)+tsin⁡(4t).

Finally, then, the general solution is given by the sum of the complementary and particular solutions. So, it can be written in any of the following forms:

  1. y=Rcos⁡(4t+ϕ)+34tcos⁡(4t)+tsin⁡(4t)

  2. y=Rsin⁡(4t+ϕ)+34tcos⁡(4t)+tsin⁡(4t)

  3. y=Acos⁡(4t)+Bsin⁡(4t)+34tcos⁡(4t)+tsin⁡(4t)

Solutions I, II, and III match the forms above. Therefore, the correct answer is "I, II, and III".
